analysis.pattern_summary: Across four rushed G3 tests (67–80%), Alexandra repeatedly loses points on sentence-level revision tasks: she changes meaning when rewriting (Q1 G3.4 "teared the flower," Q1 G3.5 "Why do the books get sold"), ignores the required structure (no "since" in G3.4 Q2, run-on comma splices in G3.3 Q4 and G3.5 Q4), and misidentifies sentence type (declarative labeled imperative). Her one-sentence responses also lack a "why" or elaboration (G3.4 Q7, Q8, Q10; G3.3 Q7), and are weakened by subject-verb agreement, verb tense, and spelling errors ("it sound," "it supporting," "beafs," "natuarl"). Paragraphs score fairly well (70–85%), so the barrier is sentence-level control and precise instruction-following rather than idea generation.
analysis.skill_gaps: subordinating conjunctions (since/because), run-on and comma splice correction, appositive construction and punctuation, fragment-to-sentence revision that preserves meaning, strong verb choice, converting statements to questions (inverted verb tense), identifying sentence types, subject-verb agreement and verb tense, explaining reasoning (the "why") in one sentence, proofreading and spelling, following prompt directions precisely
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Alexandra is marked MASTERED in nearly every G3 AlphaWrite skill, including Basic Conjunctions, Change Sentence To Question, Fragment Or Sentence, Identify Sentence Type, and Kernel Expansion, yet she still misses these task types on tests. The disconnect suggests that her mastery does not transfer to open-response writing: she completed each skill in a single attempt (with no recorded scores) and is not applying it, or checking her work, in a timed, unscaffolded setting.
analysis.rushing_impact: All four tests were flagged as rushed, and many errors (skipped required words like "since," unproofread spelling, mismatched verbs, unelaborated answers) are the type that careful rereading would likely have fixed, so rushing probably contributed substantially to the repeated failures.

analysis.pattern_summary: Ansel keeps missing the same sentence-level targets across all five G3 tests: using an appositive correctly, using a conjunction (because/but/so) to combine sentences, and turning statements into true interrogatives (G3.1 Q2, G3.2 Q3, G3.4 Q3). He often writes a run-on or comma-spliced sentence, or a fragment that ends in "!" or "," (G3.4 Q5, G3.5 Q4, Q9). His paragraphs have an opening idea and a few facts but little explanation or text evidence, and he leaves some answers unfinished or blank (G3.1 Q9, G3.5 Q11, G3.6 Q11). Informal openers ("Well..."), spelling and agreement errors, and "because" used twice in one sentence suggest weak editing and weak sentence-boundary control.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (noun + renamed noun set off by commas), combining sentences with because/but/so without run-ons, converting statements to interrogative sentences, complete sentences vs. fragments, comma splices and run-ons, answering the "why/how/what does this show" part of a prompt, paragraph development with text evidence, sentence-type identification (declarative/interrogative/exclamatory/imperative), proofreading (spelling, subject-verb agreement, formal tone), completing responses and persisting on long written tasks
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Ansel is marked MASTERED on Combine Sentences, Combine Sentences With Appositives, Write Appositives, Write Sentence From Prompt, and the paragraph skills (Elaborate Paragraphs, Transition Words), yet he still fails these exact skills on tests. Each skill has only one attempt and no recorded scores (best/latest = None), so the mastery status looks shallow or unverified and the skills are not transferring to independent, timed writing.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably hurt G3.5 (50%, with a blank paragraph and run-on answers) and likely G3.2 (a blank Q4 and weak, off-target responses), but G3.1, G3.4, and the unrushed G3.6 (blank Q11) show the same gaps and avoidance, so rushing made things worse without being the root cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): redo with a fresh attempt and a real accuracy threshold, since he keeps writing "and their names are..." or comma-spliced fragments instead of an appositive.
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G3): re-run with a focus on because/but/so and no comma splices (G3.1 Q4, G3.2 Q2, G3.5 Q3-Q4, Q9).
- Write Sentence From Prompt (Sentences G3): practice rewriting statements as true interrogatives and fragments as complete sentences, since he gave an imperative on G3.4 Q3 and left a fragment on G3.4 Q5.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): practice adding reasons and text evidence, because he restates facts without explaining "why" or "how" (G3.1 Q11, G3.2 Q11).
- Writing Brainlift: Sentence Types and Proofreading Routine (Writing Brainlift): teach the four sentence types (he left G3.2 Q4 blank), then a checklist of capital, end punctuation, one "because", spelling, and no "Well..." openers. analysis.pattern_summary: Asher passes the paragraph-length questions (Q11 at 85% on every test) but repeatedly loses points on single-sentence tasks that require precise execution: he skips directions (using "as a result" instead of because/but/so, dropping one of the two actions in a combined sentence, and omitting part of the original idea when turning a statement into a question), and he writes thin, vague ideas (appositive "my teacher," "how bad things were back then"). He also makes comprehension and inference errors (claiming the Constitution "allowed segregation") and mechanical errors (spelling such as cafiteria, eachother, dissagreed, Gradma; missing apostrophes; run-on comma splices; verb agreement; modifier placement). Because scores land at 79-89% and never fully clear mastery, the 50% and 33% sentence-level items keep him looping.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence combining with required conjunctions (because/but/so), combining sentences while retaining all ideas, appositive phrases with descriptive detail, interrogative/sentence-type transformation preserving full meaning, modifier placement and sentence revision for clarity, comma splices and run-on sentences, subject-verb and verb-tense agreement/parallelism, spelling and proofreading, apostrophes and capitalization (Kims, "studies"), text-based inference and accurate use of text details, specific/elaborated examples in single-sentence responses, following prompt directions
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The data given doesn't show AlphaWrite results, so I can't confirm specific mastered skills. Test evidence does show that he can already write organized paragraphs (85% every time) and recognizes appositive structure, yet he still misses the same skills on tests, which suggests a disconnect: he performs well in extended, open-ended writing but not in the precision tasks (following constraints, revising, proofreading) that tests demand under time pressure.
analysis.rushing_impact: All five tests were flagged as rushed, and rushing likely played a major role, since many lost points were careless (a "dddddddd" response, misspellings, ignoring the required conjunction, omitting half of a combined sentence) rather than lack of knowledge.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions (Sentences G5): he ignored the required because/but/so and dropped content when combining sentences.
- Appositives: Adding Descriptive Detail (Sentences G5): his appositives are correct in form but generic ("my teacher," "a seasoned baker"), so he needs practice making them vivid and specific.
- Revising for Clarity and Modifier Placement (Sentences G5): misplaced phrases and awkward sentences (Q5 in G5.2, Q8 in G5.1) cost points.
- Sentence Types and Transformations, including interrogative (Sentences G5): the question rewrite lost key meaning from the original sentence.
- Proofreading and Editing Checklist (Writing Brainlift): a routine to check directions, spelling, apostrophes, and agreement before submitting would reduce rushed, careless errors.

In conclusion, use anytime you have to help the monarch butterflies in surviving the long journey south.

analysis.pattern_summary: Axl's scores (58%, 89%, 78%) show he understands task prompts and writes on topic, but he loses points on sentence-level mechanics and on explaining his ideas. Specific errors include a missing question mark when rewriting a statement as a question (Q3), "that days" and an invented fact in a rewrite (Q1), "other" for "others," and a fragment that gave no reason (G3.3 Q7). He also misused "since" as a plain connector instead of a cause-and-effect link ("Layla saw a butterfly, since she took out her camera"). His answers often stop at a surface response ("she loves geodes," "fans love this event") with no reason, text evidence, or cause-and-effect reasoning. In paragraph tasks, organization and detail are inconsistent: the G3.2 paragraph was short and run-on (35%), while the G3.3 paragraph was strong (90%). Because he scores in the 50-70% range on one-sentence extended-response items, he keeps falling short of the passing threshold.
analysis.skill_gaps: end punctuation and proofreading, subordinating conjunction meaning (since/because), explaining reasons (claim plus "because"), text evidence integration, rewriting sentences for concision without adding facts, verb strengthening and precise word choice, complete-sentence responses (avoiding fragments), paragraph organization and transitions, subject-verb and plural agreement
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Axl has mastered Subordinating Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, and the Paragraphs G3 activities in AlphaWrite, yet on the G3.4 test he still used "since" incorrectly and wrote disorganized paragraphs. This suggests he can pass structured, scaffolded practice but does not transfer the skills to open-ended writing, and he does not proofread his own work. The AlphaWrite scores are also listed as None%, so mastery may reflect completion more than real proficiency.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was given, but the careless errors (a missing question mark, "that days," "go's") suggest that limited proofreading, whether from rushing or habit, probably cost him a moderate number of points.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Subordinating Conjunctions: Because/Since/Although Cause-and-Effect Rewrites (Sentences G3): he used "since" without cause-and-effect meaning, so he needs practice with the order and logic of subordinate clauses.
- Combine Sentences Quiz, retake with a focus on reasons (Combining G3): this reinforces combining ideas accurately and in a way that shows the relationship between them.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with a revision checklist (Paragraphs G3): this targets the topic sentence, supporting details, and a closing sentence, and builds a habit of checking organization.
- Writing Brainlift: Proofread and Punctuation Edit (Sentences G3): a short routine to check capitals, end marks, plurals, and verb forms before submitting.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer with a Reason (Sentences G3): practice expanding one-sentence responses with "because" and a text-based example, since he often leaves the "why" out.

Responses are often incomplete or non-attempts ("vv", "sdw") on the paragraph prompts, and the Q4 answer on G3.4 ignored the task, so it was off-task. Short responses repeatedly show sentence-fragment errors ("Because you get to throw teddy bears…"), no supporting reason or detail, and avoidable mechanics errors: misspelled words, a lowercase "i", and copying numbers or words wrongly ("454,650", "sigh", "baby"). The student also struggles with revising or combining sentences as directed (G3.2 Q1, G3.3 Q5, G3.4 Q4), where they restate or alter the text instead of applying the requested transformation.
analysis.skill_gaps: complete-sentence writing (fragments beginning with "Because"), sentence combining with because/but/so, following task directions on revise/rewrite items, proofreading and spelling (including copying from the stimulus), capitalization of "I", elaborating with reasons or details, paragraph writing from an article (main idea plus two details), text evidence integration, persistence and effort on long-response items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The student shows every G3 Combining and Paragraphs skill as MASTERED in AlphaWrite (e.g., Basic Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Write Paragraph From Prompt), yet fails the matching test items: conjunction combining (G3.4 Q4) and article-based paragraphs (G3.2 Q11, G3.3 Q11). This points to a disconnect in transfer, effort, or mastery validity (scores are listed as None%, so mastery can't be verified, and passing on 1–2 attempts is suspiciously fast). analysis.pattern_summary: Brooke repeatedly loses points on tasks that require her to apply a specific sentence-level skill: appositives (G3.1 Q1 misplaced it and produced two sentences, G3.3 Q3 gave no appositive), concise rewriting (G3.2 Q1 repeated "that day" and made a run-on), and answering exactly what the prompt asks (G3.1 Q7 gave no action, G3.3 Q5 got a transition-word item wrong at 0%). Across all three tests she also makes persistent mechanics errors that cost points even when her ideas are sound: spelling (famliy, ment, suprised, thier, kindess), capitalization ("first," "i"), comma and run-on control, and homophones (there/their). Her paragraphs (Q11, 80–85%) show good ideas and voice but weak sentence boundaries and proofreading. She scores 80–87% overall, so she is near passing and repeatedly held back by the same small, fixable errors rather than major comprehension problems.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and placement, combining sentences into one, concise rewriting (removing redundancy), run-on and comma-splice control, subordinating and transitional word choice, answering all parts of the prompt (task fidelity), capitalization of "I" and sentence starts, spelling and homophones (their/there), proofreading and self-editing, paragraph sentence boundaries and punctuation
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Brooke has mastered every AlphaWrite G3 skill, including appositives, combining sentences, conjunctions, and fragments, yet she still misses these skills on the tests (e.g., no appositive in G3.3 Q3, the run-on in G3.2 Q1, and the transition word in G3.3 Q5). This suggests the skills do not transfer to open-response, unscaffolded tasks, and that mastery came after only 1–2 attempts, which may reflect shallow practice. AlphaWrite also doesn't seem to build in editing for spelling and capitalization, which cost her on tests.
analysis.rushing_impact: The data doesn't show rushing directly, but the careless errors (uncapitalized "i," misspellings of words she knows, skipping the appositive in G3.3 Q3, and the incomplete G3.3 Q5 response) suggest rushing and a lack of proofreading likely contributed moderately to the outcomes.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G3): She misplaced the appositive on G3.1 Q1 and omitted it on G3.3 Q3, so she needs repeated practice beyond a single attempt, with extra attention to placing the appositive right after the noun.
- Write Appositives (Production G3): She needs to generate appositives independently, not just identify them, since the test task requires her to add one to a given sentence.
- Combine Sentences (Combining G3): This builds concise one-sentence rewrites without repeated phrases or run-ons, as in G3.2 Q1 and G3.1 Q1.
- Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G3): She missed the transition word on G3.3 Q5 and needs more practice choosing the best connecting word for the context.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3) plus a Writing Brainlift proofreading routine: Have her write a paragraph and then check capitalization, end punctuation, and spelling before submitting, to fix the recurring mechanics errors in her Q11 responses.

analysis.pattern_summary: Brooklyn's main gap is applying sentence-level skills in open-ended written responses. She also writes run-on sentences with comma splices and uses informal or unclear wording.

analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Brooklyn has mastered nearly every G3 skill in the plan, including appositives, basic conjunctions, and paragraph writing, yet she still misses these skills in test responses. (Quiz scores are not recorded, so mastery may reflect few attempts, with 1 attempt on several skills.)
analysis.rushing_impact: All four tests were flagged as rushed, and the blank paragraph responses, uncorrected run-ons, and passage-contradicting answers (e.g., porcupine quills) strongly suggest rushing substantially lowered her scores, so her true ability is likely higher than the results show.

analysis.pattern_summary: Carter's scores (44%, 49%, 22%, 33%) show two separate problems. The second is an engagement problem. On the 10-12 paragraph and reasoning items (Q11 and the "explain why" prompts), he repeatedly gives off-task or refusal answers ("im goood dude no thanks," "nooppeeeeeeee," "idk, sorry," "nahhhh," "......really bruh...."). These score 0-10% and are the main reason he stays in the loop. When he does engage, he gets partial credit (50-67%) with ideas that are on topic but incomplete, with no developed reason, text evidence, or complete-sentence form.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (not just recognizing it), writing complete sentences instead of fragments or phrases, giving a reason or explanation with "because," using text evidence from the passage, paragraph development (topic sentence, details, conclusion), sentence-level conventions (capitalization, spelling, run-ons), sustained effort on extended-response items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Carter has mastered every AlphaWrite skill listed, including both appositive quizzes, fragment vs. sentence, and the paragraph-writing modules, yet he still misses appositive combining and complete-sentence tasks on tests. Most skills were mastered in only 1-2 attempts with no recorded scores (best/latest = None), so the mastery may reflect low-rigor or guided practice that does not transfer to independent, passage-based writing. The data also cannot separate a skill gap from motivation, because the off-task test answers suggest he can do more than he shows.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.8 test (33%) was flagged as rushed, and its answers were short and dismissive ("nahhhh," "......really bruh....."). Rushing probably lowered that score somewhat, but the same disengagement appears on the non-rushed tests (G3.5-G3.7), so it is not the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): redo with a transfer check, because he repeatedly used "so" or "and" instead of an appositive, which suggests his earlier mastery was shallow. Require independent, scored attempts.
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3): have him write appositives from scratch in short passage contexts like the porcupine and bee items, so he practices embedding the phrase after the noun with commas.
- Fragment Or Sentence (Sentences G3): add more attempts, since he had only one and still writes fragments and phrase answers ("TO READ AND LEARN"). Pair it with a rewrite-as-complete-sentence task.
- Write Complete Sentences From Details / Write Cs From Details (Paragraphs G3): focus on sentences that state a claim plus a "because" reason, which is the pattern he misses on "explain why" questions.
- Elaborate Paragraphs and Turn Outline Into Draft (Paragraphs G3): practice with a short passage and an outline that requires text evidence, so he builds the full paragraph that Q11 asks for. Add a coach check-in or goal-setting step before each test to address the refusal responses.
analysis.priority: high. He has failed four consecutive tests with a declining trend (49% to 22% to 33%), and his off-task responses on extended-response items need a motivation or engagement intervention alongside targeted skill review.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how the solar panel project improved life in the village.

Use information from the passage to describe at least three different ways the project changed the community. Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it
questions.student_answer:
In the village, the solar panel project improved life in the village from having to use candles to having actual lights and solar panels.

There are many reasons why the solar panels made people's life in the village easier. First, the solar panels improved life in the village because when there were no solar panels, the children were unable to do their homework in the dark. When the solar panels became a thing in the village the children were now able to do their homework in the dark. Second, the shops would close later, so people can do more shopping because there is enough light in the store to shop. Third, the small medical clinic, which once closed at sunset, could store vaccines and operate equipment at night and stay open later.

The solar panels changed many peoples lives. One way how it changed many peoples lives is when people need to stay up later to do work around the house, they used to have to stop their work at sunset because they couldn't see what they were doing in the dark, solar panels fixed that. Another way it changed peoples lives was that it strengthened the spirit of cooperation among neighbors.

The people in the village were happy because their lives improved a lot. They now can spend the evenings in laughter and conversation in the streets at night with light a reminder of how progress can bring people together.

The people in the village were very grateful for the new solar panels so that their lives can b e improved.
questions.feedback: You use several accurate details from the passage, including children studying at night, shops staying open later, and the clinic storing vaccines. Your opening clearly states that solar panels replaced candles with electric light, and you also notice that neighbors became more cooperative. To strengthen your essay, explain more fully why each example improved the village instead of moving quickly from one effect to the next. For example, after mentioning the clinic, you could write, “Because the clinic could keep vaccines cold and use equipment at night, villagers could receive safer medical care when they needed it.” Keep building each body paragraph around one main benefit so your explanations can be more detailed.

skills.skill: Transformation G7 Change Sentence Type Quiz
Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Cruz repeatedly misses sentence-level grammar and structure items. Across tests he misses "What type of sentence is this?" (G7.1 Q2 and G7.2 Q2, both answered "Imperative" for declarative statements), sentence-combining (G7.3 Q3, where he picked a bare "and" join that does not show the logical relationship), and "which sentence does/doesn't belong" items (G7.2 Q7 and Q9, G7.3 Q7). His essays score a flat 70% on every Q11, and the grader notes that he lists accurate details but does not explain why they matter. He therefore plateaus in the 70s with no extended-response growth. Spelling and proofreading errors ("nescessity," "enviornment," "benifit," "taht") add to the weak polish.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence type identification (declarative vs. imperative), logical sentence combining beyond "and", relevance/topic-sentence support judgment, paragraph development and elaboration, explaining evidence (the "why it matters" link), integrating text evidence from multiple passage sections, essay introductions and conclusions, spelling and proofreading
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Cruz is marked MASTERED on Identify Sentence Type, Change Sentence Type, Combine Sentences, and Basic Conjunctions, yet he still misses the same item types on tests (sentence type, combining). He also has 5 attempts on "Essays G7 > Identify" without mastery, and the other essay stages (Draft, Outline, Polish) are mastered. His AlphaWrite mastery is not transferring to test conditions, and mastery on those stages likely reflects structure rather than depth of explanation.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data is provided, so its effect can't be determined. The repeated "Imperative" error on plainly declarative sentences suggests some careless or speedy answering, but a conceptual gap is equally plausible.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Identify Sentence Type (AlphaWrite Sentences G7): re-verify declarative vs. imperative vs. interrogative vs. exclamatory with timed, mixed-format items, since he missed this on two tests despite mastery.
- Combine Sentences / Subordinating Conjunctions (AlphaWrite Sentences G7): practice choosing the conjunction that expresses cause, contrast, or result rather than defaulting to "and" (G7.3 Q3).
- Essays G7 > Identify (AlphaWrite Essays G7): repeat with a focus on picking relevant evidence and spotting off-topic sentences, his unmastered stage and the source of the "does not belong" misses.
- Essays G7 > Draft with elaboration focus (AlphaWrite Essays G7): add "explain why this detail matters" sentences after each piece of evidence, targeting the repeated grader feedback.
- Essays G7 > Polish with proofreading checklist (AlphaWrite Essays G7): spelling and clarity pass to fix recurring errors like "nescessity" and "enviornment."

analysis.pattern_summary: Across G3.1 to G3.5 (29% to 42%), D'Sean repeatedly gives fragments or phrase-level answers ("Restaurants.", "Pet it.", "Feed it.", "yes", "because they were more noticable.") when a full sentence with a reason is required. He also misses the sentence-combining tasks, using appositives incorrectly or not at all, adding stray commas around conjunctions ("and,", "because,"), and omitting words. The 0% scores on paragraph prompts (blank or "mm"/"nhh") show that he skips or gives up on extended writing. The G3.6 score of 78% shows he can write a developed paragraph (65%) when engaged, so the loop is driven more by inconsistent effort and weak sentence-level mechanics than by a total lack of ability.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and punctuation, combining sentences with conjunctions (comma misuse, dropped words), elaborating answers with a reason or explanation, writing complete sentences instead of fragments, converting statements to questions, capitalization and proper nouns, spelling and proofreading, verb forms and subject-verb agreement ("gaven", "where climbing", "lives"), paragraph stamina and task initiation, staying on task and text (sentence 12 fragment, tail vs. quills)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows every G3 skill as MASTERED, including appositives, conjunctions, combining sentences, and paragraphs, yet he still fails those same task types on tests (G3.1 appositive, G3.2 and G3.5 conjunctions, G3.5 appositive, and blank or "mm" paragraphs). Mastery is therefore not transferring. The AlphaWrite quizzes likely have scaffolding or low-effort passes (best/latest scores show None%), and he is not applying the skills to open-ended prompts or proofreading his own work.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of five tests (G3.1, G3.4, G3.6) were rushed, and rushing likely contributed substantially to the one-word and fragment answers and unproofread errors, though the 78% on the rushed G3.6 suggests rushing alone is not the main cause. The non-rushed G3.2 and G3.5 also had blank or near-blank paragraph responses, pointing to disengagement as well.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): he fails appositive items on tests (G3.1, G3.5) despite "mastery," so redo with a higher accuracy threshold and transfer to novel sentences.
- Write Appositives (Production G3): needs practice producing appositives with correct comma placement rather than recognizing them.
- Subordinating Conjunctions / Basic Conjunctions (Sentences G3, Combining G3): to fix extra commas after "and"/"because" and dropped words when combining sentences.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): to build the habit of adding a reason or example in response to "explain why" prompts, rather than one-word answers.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): repeat with timed, no-scaffold prompts plus a proofreading checklist (capitalization, spelling, verb forms) to build stamina and stop blank or "mm" submissions.

analysis.pattern_summary: David repeatedly misses the same sentence-level tasks across all three G4 tests, even though his ideas and paragraph content are generally sound. Combining items also show errors: he leaves out words ("could on them"), adds stray commas ("so, they"), and mixes conjunctions ("because due to"). Mechanics errors appear throughout: spelling (recieved, soccar, becuase, catipiller), capitalization ("i", "texas", "africa"), and repeated words ("they they", "the it"). analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (identifying the correct noun and adding new information), sentence combining with conjunctions (because/but/so punctuation and no missing words), complete-sentence control (avoiding fragments and scrambled word order), capitalization of proper nouns and "I", spelling of common and high-frequency words, proofreading for dropped or duplicated words, elaboration/reasoning in single-sentence responses, paragraph conventions (topic sentence, supporting details, mechanics)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: David has mastered "Write Appositives," "Combine Sentences," "Basic Conjunctions," and "Change Sentence Type" in AlphaWrite, with only 1-2 attempts each, yet he still fails the matching test items (appositives, combining, exclamatory rewrite). analysis.pattern_summary: Davis writes responses that are partly right but incomplete. He gives a claim without a reason or example (Q5 "diehards," Q9 "tradition," Q6 and Q7 restating the question), and he doesn't answer the actual prompt (Q9 never says whether tossing bears is a good way to help). He also has trouble combining sentences. He uses comma splices instead of conjunctions (G3.5 Q3, Q4), picks a conjunction that changes the meaning ("because of this," Q2), ignores the directions ("yet" in Q10), and doesn't use an appositive (Q4). Paragraph responses (Q11 on both tests) lack organization, topic and concluding sentences, and conventions control. Spelling errors (animls, camals, thier, popluar, "there" for "they're", "know" for "known"), run-ons, and missed capitals recur, and these errors persist across both tests.
analysis.skill_gaps: elaboration with reasons (because/for example), answering all parts of the prompt, restating the question without adding new information, conjunction selection and meaning (cause vs. effect), following directions on required conjunctions, appositive construction, comma splices and run-ons, redundancy and concision, paragraph organization (topic sentence, transitions, concluding sentence), text evidence integration, spelling and proofreading, homophones and verb forms (there/their, know/known)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Davis is marked MASTERED in Combine Sentences, Write Appositives, Fragment or Sentence, and Unscramble Sentences, yet he still fails combining and appositive items on the tests (comma splices, no appositive, wrong conjunction). The disconnect is that he can do these skills in scaffolded, constrained AlphaWrite formats but doesn't transfer them to open-ended written responses. Each skill shows only 1 attempt, and the best/latest scores are blank (None%), so "mastered" may reflect thin evidence and not durable skill.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.2 test was rushed, and rushing probably contributed to the careless errors there (spelling, repeated time phrase, ignoring directions, unfinished answers), but the same gaps showed up on the non-rushed G3.5 test, so rushing is a moderate contributor and not the root cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3): re-run with fresh items and require transfer to open-ended writing, since he did not form an appositive on G3.5 Q4 despite "mastery."
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G3): focus on choosing and and but and so and because for the right meaning and avoiding comma splices, because he used a comma splice on Q3 and reversed cause and effect on Q2.
- Fragment Or Sentence / Run-On Sentences (Sentences G3): target comma splices and run-ons, which appear in his sentence-combining responses.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer the Question with a Reason (Paragraphs/Sentences G3): practice the "claim + because + detail" frame and fully answering the prompt, because Q5, Q6, Q7, and Q9 all lacked a reason or a direct answer.
- Writing Brainlift: Paragraph Structure and Proofreading (Paragraphs G3): practice building a topic sentence, supporting details from the text, and a concluding sentence, then a spelling and capitalization checklist, because the Q11 paragraphs were disorganized and error-filled.

questions.student_answer:
In this story, the village is nervous about getting solar panels installed. They were eventually convinced by the project leaders that solar panels were going to be good for the community. The solar panels improved life in the village in various ways, it allowed vaccines to be stored, helped children study, and boosted the economy.

First, the solar panels benefited the community by allowing vaccines to be stored overnight. Previously, they were not able to store vaccines and operate equipment at night. After the addition of solar panels to their village, they were able to do that. This clearly shows the improved village life through the solar panels.

Next, the solar panels supported the community by helping children study. Before solar, children who wanted to study in the evening had to strain their eyes. After solar was installed, children no longer had to strain their eyes every evening to study. This clearly shows the benefits of solar panels.

Finally, the solar panels helped the community by boosting the economy. The shops used to have to close at sunset. After the addition of solar, they could stay open after the sun went down. In turn, this benefited the economy and clearly shows the benefits of the addition of solar panels.

The solar panels improved life in the village in various ways.This is clearly illustrated in the benefits of: vaccines being able to be stored overnight, children being able to study in the evenings without straining their eyes, and boosting the economy by helping shops stay open longer. Solar is clealy a massive benefit!

Write an **expository essay** explaining how the bike lane project improved life in the town.

questions.student_answer:
Wouldn't safer streets be better? In this passage, the author talks about a town that decided to add bike lanes, and the effects it had. The bike lane improved life in the town in several ways.

First, it helps students get to school. It was dangerous for students to bike to school because they had to hug the curb. With the addition of bike lanes, they did not have to hug the curb, and had plenty of space to ride. This allowed children to bike to school more often and safer. This improved life in the town by helping safety.

Second, the number of minor crashes went down. This saves people money, and makes the town a safer place. People saving money mean the bike lane pays for itself. Also, with fewer accidents, people are in a better mood. This clearly shows that the bike lane was a huge benefit for safety and community happiness.

Finally, children could play outside for longer before dinner. This is because cars drove slower. Parents felt more comfortable keeping their kids out even when there was less visibility. This improves life in the town by keeping children more active and healthy.

The bike lane improved life in the town in several ways. Shown through helping students get to school, lowering the number of minor crashes, and having children play outside for longer. Don't you want a bike lane now?

incorrect_questions.student_answer:

questions.student_answer:
Whisting to speak is interesting right? In the passage "More Than a Whistle" People used to whistle over long distances, and that specific language is still being perserved in the modern era. The language of El Silbo Gomero is more than just a whistle.

First, Silbo is more practical than a whistle because it was used to communicate. It was not just a tune that people hummed, it was a language. It was used so that people could talk over long distances. From hill to hill, it went much further thn a shout could, "El Silbo was a necessity rather than a curiosity." Clearly, It's not just a whistle, it is a whole language.

In addition, Silbo is more important than simply a whistle becuase it carries historical significance. As well as being a modern day reminder of what they used to use, it also respects the tradition, as shown when "adults use it only for cultural events." Kids like the young whistler Cyro take pride in "carrying the voice of their ancestors through the mountain air." All of this makes it more important than a basic whistle.

Finally, Silbo is more interesting than a whistle becuase it is unique. the text does not mention it being used in other places, which would make it exclusive to Gomera. It is also used "to entertain tourists," which shows it is rare, becuase something commonplace is not used to entertain people.

In conclusion, El Silbo Gomero is much more than an average whistle. It is communication, due to its use in speech over long distances, tradition becuase it carries historical significance through traditions, and unique to Gomero, becuase it is seen nowhere else in the world. Wouldn't it be cool to be able to hear a language made completely out of whistles?
questions.feedback: You clearly explain that El Silbo helped people communicate “from hill to hill” and that young people such as Cyro take pride in carrying on an ancestral tradition. Your five-paragraph structure and transitions such as “First,” “In addition,” and “Finally” make your ideas easy to follow. To strengthen your essay, explain more directly how each detail connects people to one another or to their past, instead of mainly repeating that El Silbo is “more than a whistle.” For example, after describing required school classes, you could write, “Because every student learns El Silbo, the island’s younger generation shares the same tradition as earlier generations.” Be careful not to make unsupported claims, such as saying El Silbo exists nowhere else, when the passage does not state that.

analysis.pattern_summary: Declan's scores are clustered at 80-83%, and the only visible loss on each test is the Q11 expository essay (70%, 80%, 70%) plus a missed Q3 sentence-combining item on G7.2. His essays have the right structure (three benefits, transitions, body paragraphs), but the intros are weak. They either retell the passage ("In this story, the village is nervous...") or open with a casual rhetorical question ("Wouldn't safer streets be better?", "...interesting right?") instead of a clear thesis. They also have surface errors (comma splice "in various ways, it allowed...", misspellings "Whisting"/"perserved") and, judging by the truncated feedback, thin elaboration of how each detail supports the claim. The Q3 miss suggests he isn't reliably choosing the logical or causal relationship between ideas.
analysis.skill_gaps: thesis statement and intro writing for expository essays, formal academic tone (avoiding rhetorical questions and "right?"), paragraph elaboration and explaining the "so what" of evidence, comma splices and run-ons, proofreading and spelling, cause-effect logic when combining sentences, sentence variety and flow
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Declan is marked mastered in all the sentence-level skills (conjunctions, combining at G3/G6/G7, sentence type, fragments, appositives, kernel expansion, elaborating paragraphs), yet he still misses a G7 combine-sentences item and makes run-on and comma-splice errors in essays. This suggests he completes the isolated drills but doesn't transfer them to extended writing or to choosing the most logical combination. The AlphaWrite scores are also all listed as None%, so I can't tell how strong the mastery was (e.g., whether it was reached in a single attempt).
analysis.rushing_impact: All three tests were flagged as rushed, and the errors seen (spelling, comma splice, informal openers, a likely careless Q3 choice) are the kind rushing causes, so it probably cost him a significant share of the 10-20 points he is missing, possibly enough to change the outcome given how close he is.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Writing Thesis Statements for Expository Essays (Writing Brainlift / Essay Foundations): his intros summarize the passage or use rhetorical questions instead of stating a clear, formal controlling idea.
- Elaborate Paragraphs with Evidence + Explanation (AlphaWrite Paragraph Development G7): his essays

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how students learn new languages in effective ways.

Use information from the passage to support your ideas.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it**: Support each point with facts or examples from the passage and explain what they show (5 points)

**Stay organized and on topic**
questions.student_answer: In a busy neighborhood café, people speak many different languages. A family at one table talks in Spanish. At the counter, a worker sings along to a French song on the radio. Scenes like this happen across the United States, a country shaped by immigrants. Even though English is the most common school language, many Americans grow up using two languages at home and in their communities. Learning multiple languages can help people in many different ways. Studies show it can help with memorization and improve resilience and problem-solving skills. Studies also show that infants and younger kids learn faster and have an easier time using proper pronunciation. As a result, many families have started teaching kids second languages while they are infants. One of many ways children can learn is through immersion. Immersion is a class where the teachers use the language during all parts of the day, from simple conversation to learning new subjects. Using the immersion method can help kids hear the language and figure out the vocabulary. One other helpful method uses real communication. Some classrooms connect students with pen pals across the globe. When students reach out to them, they create a bond. This bond can help kids find motivation to learn their language to understand the culture of their pen pal. In conclusion, learning a second language is important for understanding immigrants and peers. Learning a new language can help a child grow their brain and understand others' culture. Languages can be taught in multiple different ways, including immersion and talking to pen pals. Children can also be taught at a young age to make pronunciation easier. Languages have many purposes in a child's brain, but the main reason is to help others share culture and feel welcome.
questions.feedback: You clearly explain several effective ways students can learn languages, including starting young, using immersion, and communicating with pen pals. Your explanation that pen pals can motivate students to practice so they can understand another culture is especially strong. To make your essay easier to follow, separate it into five paragraphs: an introduction with your main claim, one paragraph for each learning method, and a conclusion. This structure will help each important idea stand out and give your reader clear pauses between your points.

Write an **expository essay** explaining how teamwork helped restore the Mithi River and what the community learned from this experience.

**Use evidence and explain it**: Support each poi
questions.student_answer:
For many years, the Mithi River in Mumbai, India, was full of trash. Factories dumped waste into the water. Sewage flowed in every day. The river turned black, and it smelled so bad that people stayed away.

When hope seemed lost, a group called Earth5R showed up. They wanted to return the river to its original beauty. They knew it would take hard work and sacrifice. They also knew they could not do it alone.

First, the group mapped out the river and marked the parts that needed the most cleaning. They took water samples to see where the waste was affecting the river most. Then, they held a volunteer event where anyone could come and help the river flourish. At first, few community members came. But soon, more and more people joined. After a few months, the group had removed over fourteen tonnes of trash.

Over time, the river began to return to its original state. Tests showed the water was twenty percent cleaner than before! Eventually, the community started hanging out near the river again.

The project helped the community grow and flourish. It taught the people that everyone should play their part, and not just let the professionals handle it. Volunteers learned to work together as a community and realize that regular people can take action too. Currently, the community holds cleanups to maintain the river's condition and keep it the same for years.
questions.feedback: You clearly describe how Earth5R brought volunteers together, especially when you explain that more people joined the cleanup and removed “over fourteen tonnes of trash.” Your final paragraph also thoughtfully explains the community’s lesson that regular people can take action instead of waiting for professionals. To make your explanation stronger, add more sentences that show why each example of teamwork mattered, not just what happened. For example, after describing the cleanup, you could write, “Because families, schools, and shops worked together, they could remove far more trash than Earth5R could have removed alone.”

analysis.pattern_summary: Eric repeatedly misses the targeted sentence-manipulation items (appositives, combining sentences, and converting statements to questions) and gets only partial credit on one-sentence responses, which are mostly clear but lack a "because" reason. His paragraph-level responses (Q11 on each test: 30%, 90%, 60%) show inconsistent organization, with run-on sentences, comma splices, missing end punctuation, and ideas that are listed rather than developed or tied to the article's central idea. Recurring conventions errors (capitalizing "I," spelling, "brang," "a/an," doubled words, comma use, missing question marks) keep otherwise adequate content below mastery. Eric also seems to misread or only partly follow the directions on transformation tasks, for example by answering with a story sentence instead of adding an appositive, or by describing the geode instead of turning the sentence into a question.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction, combining sentences into a single sentence (not two with a period), converting statements to interrogatives (G3.4 Q3), supporting claims with a "because" reason, writing complete sentences (no fragments or run-ons), comma splice and end-punctuation control, capitalization and spelling proofreading, past-tense and verb forms, paragraph development with a topic sentence and elaboration, integrating text evidence from articles, following task directions precisely
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Eric is marked MASTERED on Write Appositives, Combine Sentences, Change Sentence To Question, Fragment Or Sentence, and the paragraph skills, but he still fails these same skills on tests (G3.1 Q1, G3.3 Q3 and Q4, G3.4 Q3). The AlphaWrite skills were each attempted only once and show no recorded scores, so mastery was probably reached on easy or scaffolded items and does not transfer to independent, text-based writing or careful reading of the directions.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided, but the many careless errors (missing question marks, "owe" for "own," doubled "playing," unfinished sentences) suggest limited proofreading that probably cost him a moderate amount of credit, though it does not explain the repeated misses on appositive and combining tasks.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3), repeated with independent, higher-difficulty items: Eric missed appositive and combine items on G3.1 and G3.3, so his earlier single-attempt mastery needs to be re-verified with multiple attempts.
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G3): he left two separate sentences on G3.3 Q4 and G3.1 Q1, so he needs practice merging them with commas, conjunctions, or appositives.
- Change Sentence To Question (Sentences G3): he rewrote the statement instead of making it an interrogative (G3.4 Q3) and omitted question marks, so he needs practice with word order, auxiliary verbs, and end punctuation.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3), with article-based prompts: his Q11 paragraphs lack a developed central idea and use run-ons, so he needs practice with a topic sentence, supporting details, and a closing sentence.
- Writing Brainlift: Add a Reason with "Because" and a Proofreading Checklist (Sentences/Paragraphs G3): most of his one-sentence responses lose credit for lacking a reason or for capitalization, spelling, and comma errors.

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Intro
questions.student_answer:
Most people believe that self-driving cars will be the future of transportation. They believe this because they will allow people who cannot drive to have the freedom to travel. However, it is important for people to understant both the benefits and the concerns of self-driving cars before they become more common.

First, let's talk about the benefits of new self-driving cars. One benefit is that self-driving cars should stay focused and stop crashes caused by human error. The self-driving aspect of it would allow people who might not be able to drive, like elderly or disabled people, to have the freedom to travel again. Self-driving cars give many benefits to the community.

On the otherhand, many people have concerns about self-driving cars. One concern is what happens if a car fails? In one driving test conducted in Arizona, the car sensed the person but fail to stop in time. One other concern is that many people will lose their jobs. Right now in the USA, millions of people work driving cars and trucks. In summary, tons of people have concerns about self-driving cars, such as that many people will lose their jobs.

There are also some legal questions about self-driving cars. Such as, what happens when a self-driving car gets into a crash? Who would be to blame? The owner? The manufacturer? The software company? Who would the other rider sue? These questions also need to be answered before self-driving cars become more common.

It's important for people to understand the benefits and concerns before making a desision, or explaining the conflict to other people. Self-driving cars, like all new inventions, should always be questioned before becomming common. The benefits and concerns for making any new product or invention are always important for people to understand, so that they can grasp what they are voting for.

analysis.pattern_summary: Hayden's scores sit at 78–81% across G4.1–G4.3, and nearly every item is a one-sentence or paragraph response scored at 67–75%. The same mechanical errors recur on every test: spelling (Kenye, collage, wich, sping, tadition, dicoverd, doug), homophones (their/there), capitalization (Is, i've, christmas, Lastly), and punctuation or run-ons (missing comma, "dayso"). Sentences are also often thin or tangled. Responses stop at a basic claim with no reason or detail ("lead by example and be nice"; "building things"). Revisions break syntax ("which I thought was really it was very cool"), and combined sentences are long and awkward. Hayden doesn't proofread or elaborate, so he stays stuck just under the mastery threshold, and the gaps are in editing and sentence quality rather than comprehension. The paragraph responses (70–85%) are organized, with transitions like First/Then/Lastly, but they are marred by conventions errors, repeated words ("have much have much"), and possessive mistakes.
analysis.skill_gaps: spelling of grade-level and high-frequency words, homophone/word choice (their/there), capitalization (sentence starts, "I", holidays), comma use in compound/complex and appositive sentences, run-on and fused sentence correction, sentence elaboration (adding reasons/details), sentence clarity and revision, possessive apostrophes, proofreading/self-editing, concise combining of sentences with because/but/so, paragraph conclusion and detail development, fragment-to-sentence conversion

The mastery appears to be on structured, isolated tasks and does not transfer to independent, unprompted writing where he must self-edit, and no AlphaWrite skills cover spelling or proofreading.

- Expanding Sentences with Reasons and Details (Sentences G4): Hayden's one-sentence answers repeatedly lack a "because" reason or example, which graders flag each time.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G4/G5): the appositive comma was missed on G4.1 Q3, and commas around appositives need practice.

analysis.pattern_summary: Hudson's tests show a consistent gap between his ideas and his sentence-level execution. He generally understands the content but loses points to missing words ("have to something different," "can live Texas"), subject-verb and tense errors ("Did shawl dances began," "the road can be dangourous"), comma splices, and run-on constructions. He also struggles with sentence-combining and fragment-expansion items (appositives, subordinate clauses, word-order fixes), which are mostly capped at 50%. His one-sentence responses often answer vaguely, without the specific explanation or text-based reason the prompt asks for (G4.4 Q9, G4.5 Q6/Q7, G4.6 Q10). His paragraphs have a clear claim but little elaboration or text evidence, and he leans on a formulaic "That is why…" conclusion.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction, comma splices and run-ons, fragment-to-sentence expansion, complex sentences with subordinating conjunctions, verb tense and agreement (base form after "did"), proofreading for omitted words, capitalization and spelling (homophones such as there/their and no/know), word-order revision, specific text-based explanations in one-sentence responses, paragraph elaboration and evidence integration, answering the "why" or "how" in the prompt
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Combine Sentences is marked mastered in AlphaWrite, but with only 1 attempt and no recorded best or latest score, the mastery signal is weak. Tests still show repeated failures on combining, appositives, and complete-sentence construction, so the skill is not transferring to open-response writing or to his own proofreading.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a modest effect, since G4.4 and G4.6 scores (81% and 77%) are in line with his non-rushed tests, though the omitted words and misspellings (e.g., "buit," "trafic") and the vague G4.4 Q9 answer look like carelessness.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G4/G5): he writes comma splices or skips the appositive on G4.5 Q3 and G4.4 Q3, and his single mastery attempt needs re-verification with more practice.
- Fix Fragments and Run-On Sentences (Sentences G4): he struggles with fragment expansion (G4.2 Q2/Q3, G4.4 Q2, G4.1 Q4) and with comma splices.
- Subordinating Conjunctions and Complex Sentences (Sentences G4): sentences starting with "If" and "Since" are left incomplete or garbled.
- Proofread and Revise Your Own Sentences (Writing Brainlift): a self-editing checklist (missing words, capitals, verb form, homophones) would target recurring slips such as "have to something," "Did…began," "there/their," "no/know."
- Paragraph Elaboration with Text Evidence (Paragraphs G4): he needs to add specific details and quotations to support claims in the G4.x Q11 responses and to answer the "why" in the one-sentence text-based items.

analysis.pattern_summary: Iker has trouble following the specific transformation a prompt asks for. He rewrites sentences instead of turning them into questions (G3.2 Q3, G3.5 Q1, G3.4 Q3), ignores the required conjunction or appositive (G3.4 Q2 "since", G3.5 Q4, G3.6 Q3), and gives a wrong or off-task response on identification items (G3.2 Q4 "imperative", G3.5 Q5, G3.4 Q1 where he wrote a paragraph instead of changing a verb). His one-sentence responses are often fragments or loosely connected to the prompt ("Resilient, adventurous, and remember"; "To stay in place so you can read"; "they have quills"). Conventions errors also appear throughout: its/it's, subject-verb agreement, "would of", and spelling. He also left several items blank (G3.2 Q5, Q8), so the scores reflect incomplete attempts as well as skill gaps. Scores stuck at 28–51% across four tests show the same problems repeating.
analysis.skill_gaps: converting statements to questions (interrogative transformation), sentence type identification, using specified subordinating conjunctions (since/because) with correct clause direction, writing appositives (renaming noun phrase set off with commas), identifying appositives in text, fragment-to-complete-sentence revision, writing complete sentences with subject and verb in short responses, giving a reason that answers "why" using text evidence, following task directions and staying on-prompt, subject-verb and noun-number agreement, its/it's and basic spelling/usage (would have), task persistence (blank responses)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Iker shows MASTERED on nearly every G3 skill, including appositives, combining sentences, fragments, and unscrambling, yet he still misses these same skills on tests (e.g., appositive combining at 50% and appositive identification at 0%). The AlphaWrite records show no scores (best/latest = None) and only 1–2 attempts each, so mastery was probably reached on scaffolded, low-volume practice that does not transfer to unscaffolded test prompts.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a moderate effect: the rushed G3.4 and G3.5 tests contain off-task, rambling, or unfinished answers and careless errors (spelling, agreement, its/it's), but the unrushed G3.2 test scored the same 36%, so rushing is not the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Sentence From Prompt (Sentences G3): Iker answers off-task or turns in blank responses, so he needs repeated practice reading a directive and producing exactly the requested sentence, including statement-to-question and verb-change rewrites.
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): he joins ideas with "and" instead of using an appositive, so he should redo this with a higher mastery threshold and varied noun phrases.
- Identify Appositives (Sentences G3): he gave a summary instead of the appositive on G3.5 Q5, so he needs repeated retrieval practice that requires him to locate and quote the phrase.
- Basic Conjunctions Quiz (Combining G3): the same skill needs retesting with because, since, but, and so, with emphasis on which clause follows the conjunction (G3.4 Q2, G3.6 Q2).
- Fragment Or Sentence (Sentences G3): he writes new run-on content in place of fixing fragments and gives fragment answers to "why" questions, so he needs practice with subject and verb and with restating the question stem in his answer.

analysis.pattern_summary: Jackson handles long, well-organized paragraph prompts well (Q11 scores of 55%, 85%, 90%). He loses most of his points on short, single-sentence responses, where he writes sentence fragments ("Because every page kids could write thier names," "A beautiful geode, a rock with…," "How many bears people can take") and answers that don't fully address the prompt. He often names an idea without explaining why or how it matters (G3.4 Q6, Q8, Q10). He also struggles with sentence transformation tasks: his questions don't match the source sentence, he leaves a conjunction combination unfinished, and he makes spelling and mechanics errors (thier, beacuse, its/it's, goledn).
analysis.skill_gaps: complete sentence construction (fragment vs. sentence), sentence transformation (declarative to interrogative that keeps the original content), combining sentences with conjunctions, appositive phrases, explaining reasoning (the "why" or "because" elaboration), responding directly to the prompt in one sentence, character analysis in a full statement, spelling and mechanics (their, because, it's, proofreading), paragraph fluency and sentence variety (G3.2 choppy sentences)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite data wasn't included, so I can't confirm specific mastery there. The test pattern itself points to a disconnect: Jackson performs well on extended paragraph writing (85–90%) but repeatedly fails the short, precise sentence-level items. This suggests that paragraph-level practice isn't transferring to sentence-level accuracy, or that he doesn't proofread and self-check short responses.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided, but the unfinished answer ("The book had golden spines,"), the many misspellings, and the incomplete fragments suggest that rushing or lack of proofreading likely contributed moderately to the lost points.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fragments vs. Complete Sentences (Sentences G3): Jackson repeatedly writes fragments beginning with "Because" or noun phrases, so he needs practice identifying and fixing missing subjects and verbs.
- Rewrite Statements as Questions (Sentences G3): his interrogatives drift from the original content (geode, books), so he needs practice keeping the key subject and details while changing the sentence type.
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions (Sentences G3): he left the conjunction task incomplete (0%), so he needs practice joining two details with "and," "but," or "so."
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3/G4): his appositive attempt was close but imprecise ("amazing sellers" didn't keep the original meaning), so he needs practice with the structure and with preserving meaning.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer + Reason Sentence Frames (Writing Brainlift): he states an idea but omits why it matters (G3.4 Q6, Q8, Q10), so he should practice a "claim + because" frame and a proofreading checklist (complete sentence, answers the question, spelling check).

analysis.pattern_summary: Jacob repeatedly misses the specific sentence-level task the prompt asks for. He writes a statement when asked for a question (G3.1 Q2, G3.9 Q4), skips or substitutes for the required conjunction (because/but/so) or appositive (G3.1 Q4, G3.6 Q3, G3.2 Q10, G3.9 Q5), and leaves some items blank (G3.1 Q4, G3.5 Q2). His one-sentence responses are usually on topic but lack developed reasons, and they carry persistent mechanics errors: missing end punctuation, lowercase "I" or sentence starts, subject-verb agreement, fragments, and spelling. His paragraphs score 60-90% but include run-ons, fragments, and loosely supported or inaccurate details.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence combining with because/but/so, appositive construction and identification, converting statements to questions (including the question mark), following the exact directions of a prompt, subject-verb agreement, complete sentences vs. fragments, capitalization and end punctuation, spelling of high-frequency and grade-level words, elaborating with reasons or explanations, paragraph development and accuracy of text evidence, sentence type identification, task persistence on blank or skipped items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: "Change Sentence Type" is marked mastered in AlphaWrite from a single attempt with no recorded score, yet Jacob still fails to turn statements into questions (G3.1 Q2, G3.9 Q4, G3.6 Q4) and misidentifies sentence types (G3.2 Q4). The mastery does not transfer to timed, text-based test items, and the one-attempt record suggests it may be unreliable.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing very likely contributed substantially. Most tests were flagged rushed, and many errors are careless ones (missing punctuation and capitals, typos, blank responses, ignoring the required connector) that a quick self-check would catch, though the repeated conjunction and appositive misses also show real skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Because, But, and So (Sentences G3): Jacob repeatedly omits or replaces the required conjunction (G3.1 Q4, G3.2 Q10, G3.9 Q5).
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3): he confuses appositives with conjunctions or whole phrases (G3.5 Q5, G3.6 Q3, G3.1 Q1).
- Change Sentence Type, re-practice with multiple attempts and question-mark/punctuation checks (Sentences G3): the existing mastery is based on a single attempt and doesn't show on tests.
- Subject-Verb Agreement and Fragment Repair (Grammar/Sentences G3): errors like "Our dog have" and fragments like "To show a sign of warning..." recur.
- Writing Brainlift revision and proofreading routine (Writing Brainlift): a checklist covering directions, capital letters, end punctuation, spelling, and adding a "because" reason would address the rushed, careless errors and thin elaboration.

skills.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Jagger writes clear, well-organized paragraphs (Q11 scores of 85–95% on three tests), but he repeatedly loses points on sentence-level tasks. He doesn't construct appositives; in G4.1 and G4.2 he adds a prepositional or comma-separated phrase instead of renaming the noun. He also makes subject-verb agreement errors with compound and singular subjects ("dedication and impact… was," "A wildflower… are"), comma errors when combining sentences ("because his efforts, enrollment has doubled"), and logic and copying slips ("so predators could get it," "steady" for "ready"). In G4.4 the paragraph dropped to 50% because it stated a general lesson without specific text details.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, subject-verb agreement (compound and singular subjects), comma use in combined sentences, sentence-combining with because/but/so, fragment expansion into complete sentences, proofreading and editing (spelling and copying accuracy), logical coherence of cause-and-effect clauses, specific text evidence and detail in paragraphs, precise word choice
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows all 15 skills as MASTERED (Combine Sentences, Kernel Expansion, Fragment Or Sentence, Subordinating Conjunctions, and others), with no best or latest percentages recorded and mostly 1 attempt each. Yet he still misses the same skills on tests: combining sentences, expanding fragments, and conjunctions. The mastery appears to reflect shallow, recognition-level, or one-attempt completion and doesn't transfer to constructed written responses. Appositives aren't clearly covered by any mastered skill, so that is a coverage gap.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of four tests were rushed (G4.1, G4.2, G4.4), and the many careless errors (agreement, spelling, copying "steady," stray commas) suggest rushing moderately to substantially contributed. The non-rushed G4.3 still scored only 88%, though, so rushing is not the sole cause. Skill gaps in sentence-level control remain.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Appositive Phrases / Combine Sentences Using Appositives (AlphaWrite Sentences): he scored 0% on G4.2 Q4 and 50% on G4.1 Q3 because he added prepositional phrases rather than renaming appositives set off by commas.
- Subject-Verb Agreement with Compound and Singular Subjects (AlphaWrite Grammar): errors like "dedication and impact… was" and "wildflower… are" recur when he expands fragments.
- Combine Sentences with Because/But/So and Comma Rules (AlphaWrite Sentences, reattempt with accuracy threshold): he makes comma splices and misplaced commas, and one attempt did not produce durable mastery.
- Kernel Expansion and Fragment Repair, Complete Sentence Revision (AlphaWrite): he needs practice turning noun-phrase fragments into complete sentences with a correct predicate and agreement.
- Writing Brainlift: Proofread and Revise Checklist plus Text Evidence Elaboration: a pre-submit check for agreement, commas, spelling, and copying accuracy, plus adding specific details from the text (as in G4.4) to support a lesson or claim.

questions.student_answer:
Solar power, a new inovative technology that captures the energy from the sun, has now been set up in a off the grid rural town. This town previously had not had electricity but community led projects pushed for widespread solar panel setup on all the residents roofs. Before these solar panels were installed the town had to run by candles and fire for illumination. These solar panels changed how the town functioned, now shops could stay open later, and the clinic could store medicine over night. This tranformation has inspired other towns with similar situations to consider the solar panel concept.

Before the solar panels were installed, the town was dark at night, and kids and buissneses had to close early or function by firelight. The community members discovered solar panels and thought it was a good fit for the community. That qoute shows one of the biggest probems that a lack of power presents, and the new solar panels solved this problem.

Once the panels were insltaled, people were curious about how to take care of them and keep them running. The community started to run workshops to teach the towns families how to clean, maintain and understand the power from the solar panels. In the 3rd paragraph of the story they state, "However, the transformation was not without challenges...project leaders organized workshops on panel care and energy saving habits." In this quote it shows how the residents were concered but with these frequent workshops all their questions and concerns were solved.

The town has now become a model for sustainable living as it uses renuable energy for all of the towns needs. The residents take pride in their solar panel setups, and how they were one of the first to adpot the technology. In the last paragraph of the story they say, "The shift to solar energy not only improved daily life-it also strengthened the spirt of cooperation among neighbors." In that sentence they say how it also stregthed the community bond beacuse they all participated in a large pionering project that broght them together. The town has benifited in more ways than just improving their own life, but inspiring and bringing others toghther.

In conclusion, this town has evolved from candlelight to inspiring people to set up solar for themselves. They now have power at night for the residents, stores, and hospitals so they can open and stay up after dark. This large transformative project has broght the town community closer. Finaly, this solar project improved this small village by a large amount and a story for others to get inspired.

incorrect_questions.prompt:

Write an **expository essay** explaining how the bike lane project improved life in the town.

incorrect_questions.student_answer:
You have probably seen a bike lane, but this town had never and it just happend to change their whole community. This town decided to add bike lanes after people felt unsafe riding or walking. When the new bike lanes were added the drivers slowed and there was more foot traffic. Shops and schools saw more people walking or riding to get places and parents said they felt calmer knowing that their kids were safe. This small change turned the community around making the streets slower and giving more space for pedestrians and bikers.

At first, these streets were busy beacuse people were driving instead of walking everywhere. Once the bike lanes were installed the streets shrunk and more people were encoraged to walk and bike. In the second paragraph of the story they say, "Students could bike to school without hugging the curb." This shows an example of how people can commute safely to and from school. This can go back to the idea that this town had a community upgrade beacuse you start seeing more faces on the street.

At first shops and local buissnes started to get more people passing by their stores before and after work. You may ask why and that beacuse the paths people commuted on were passing these local shops. This caused them to open longer hours so they could accomodate the influx in customers. In paragraph two of the story they say, "Shops stayed open later, and more customers stopped by on their way home." This shows how these bike lanes really gave more incentive to be outside and interacting with the local community.

With this change in the community structure that included the new bike lanes parents and kids also found a benifit from this change. Parents let kids stay out longer in the afternoon beacuse of the increased trust. In the second paragraph of the story, "Parents said the streets felt calmer in the evening, and children could play outside for longer before dinner." This shows how the parents had more trust in the community even during darker or more unsafe hours. You can bring all of this back to how these bike lanes give more trust not just in families but in the community as a whole.

From kids biking to school to pedestrians stopping on their way home from work these bike lanes change the whole comminity. In conclusion, a simple thing like restructuring a road can really change a community as a whole.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses an appositive?
questions.student_answer: B. Cyro, was a young islander, who loved his goats.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
The question refers to the passage "More Than a Whistle" (Stimulus S1).

Write an **expository essay** explaining how El Silbo connects the people of La Gomera to their past and to one another.

Support your explanation with evidence from at least three different parts of the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it
questions.student_answer:
On the canary islands near the coast of africa there is a island that has a very special way of ancient comunication. In this small island community on La Gomera use a form a whisting to communicate to other villagers called El SIlibo. This language consits of a variation in pitches or lengthes of each whistle that can be herd up to two miles away. We dont know when this language first started but we know that they created it as a way to comunicate things like news, invitations and warnings. This language has been slowly disapering though the years but the spanish goverment is working to conserve it.

La Gomera known for its grand valleys and steep clifs has on of the most special and unique local languages there has ever come to be. The small island community usees whistles with diffrent tones to comunicate messages across the island. While we dont know when this language was created we know that they used this language to communitcate messages to the whole island though the valleys and hills. The language consits of each vowel and consanant being convered into a sound that and be whistled and heard across the rugged landscape of the island. It has been used for centuries but has slowly started to fade.

Around the 1980s less and less people were useing El silibo beacuse of the phone system. The Spanish government saw that the island was at risk of lousing this special language that was essential to keeping the culture alive. Now El silibo calsses are a required course in school. These classes teach students how to whistle and perfect their El Silibo skills. Some kids like Cyro prowdly whislte though the streets showing the pride in his ancestors.

Even though El Silibo is taught in schools it is still not the most spoken language. El Silibo is most used for entertainment for tourists or at cultural events but it is still very important as to the people as they can demonstarte their heritage and pride for their ancestors. This can make this forgotten language feel more intigrated into the islands history and culture. This shows that even though it is no longer a useful language the local residents find ways of keeping their language alive.

In conclusion El Slibo is a very important part of undersnading how cultures can evolve languages for special situations and occasions. Before phones El Silibo was more nessicary to know how to communicate though the island. In the end kids like Cyro will keep the legacy of their ancestors going on though generations and people will always we intertained and curious about El SIlibo.
questions.feedback: You did a really thoughtful job explaining El Silbo, especially your insight that 'even though it is no longer a useful language the local residents find ways of keeping their language alive' — that shows you understood how the whistle connects people to their ancestors, not just how it works. Your essay is well built too, moving clearly from the language's origins, to its 1980s decline, to how young whistlers like Cyro keep it alive today. The main thing to work on next is proofreading your sentences so a reader never has to stop and re-read. A few phrases lost their meaning because of small missing or extra words, like 'use a form a whisting to communicate' and 'sound that and be whistled' — reading your draft aloud will help you catch spots where a word is missing or doubled. Once your sentences are tightened up, you can do a second read just for spelling and capitalizing names like the Canary Islands, Africa, and Spanish. Your ideas are strong, so cleaning up these details will let them shine even more.
