questions.title: Multiple choice (single answer)
questions.prompt:
Which option combines the two ideas logically?

**Idea 1**: *Starting a community garden is not always easy*.

**Idea 2:** *Many cities offer support to help communities succeed*.
questions.student_answer: D. Because starting a community garden is not always easy, many cities offer support.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Read the passage ***From Empty Lots to Community Gardens***.

Write an **expository essay** **explaining which three benefits** of community gardens have the **greatest impact on life in cities**.

Explain why each benefit matters, using evidence from at least three different parts of the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence a
questions.student_answer:
When you think of a lively community, you probably don't think of an abanonded parking lot. In many communities around the U.S. people have started projects converting abandoned lots into community gardens that benifit the community in many ways. These gardens provide fresh produce to a community which sometimes hard to find. These community spaces can bring people in the neighborhood together and gives safe place to meet new people. The enviorment also benifits from a community garden as plants absorb carbon dioxide and soil absorbs water to reduce runoff. There is many ways community gardens are helping communities so lets dive deeper in some examples.

You will find empty plots of land in neighborhoods all over the U.S., these places can feel sad and lifeless but a new project aims to give them new life. Gardeners and community members have started converting old land plots into community gardens as a shared space and place for people to contrubute and learn. In the 2nd paragraph of the passage they state ,"Neighbors work side by side to plant seeds water crops and care for the soil." As stated in the passage these places let all neighbors work together to a big common goal which brings the community closer. These gardens not only bring people together but it brings everyone together in good health.

On a topic of good health many cities lack fresh produce because of food deserts. Communty gardens provide free accesible produce to the community that works hard on growing it. As stated in the 2nd paragraph of the passage, "for many families, fresh produce can be expensive or hard to find." This shows how people want produce but is is not so simple in parts of the U.S and these gardens help with that. These gardens not only help people thay healthy but also the envoirment.

These community gardens also benifit the envoirment as plants and trees help with all sorts of envormental issues. Plants and trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air as there is lots of carbon dioxide in cities. The gardens also absorb water in the soil to reduce runoff. And as stated in the 5th paragraph of the passage, "They also give insecs and birds a place to live in crowded cities." Just one garden can give a handfull of benefits not just to all aspects of nature but the community too.

In conclusion community gardens can help relive a dead plot of land in a community and make it beneficial for all. These gardens help the envoirment from reducing carbon dioxide and giving animals a place to live. They also creat fresh accesible produce for a whole community. All of this while bringing a community together in the procces creating new friends and better neighbor interactions. Finnaly every community should put in the time for one of these great gardens not just for them but for everyone.
questions.feedback: You wrote an exceptionally well-structured five-paragraph essay that clearly explains the community, health, and environmental benefits of community gardens. Your integration of evidence from multiple parts of the text is strong, and your explanations effectively connect each fact to its broader impact. To take your writing to the next level, set aside time at the end to carefully proofread for common spelling patterns like 'environment' and 'benefit.' Additionally, be sure to watch out for comma splices between complete thoughts and check for subject-verb agreement in phrases like 'there are many ways.'

questions.student_answer: B. Imperative

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
The question uses the passage "The Robotics Club That Changed a School" (Stimulus S1).

Read the passage ***The Robotics Club That Changed a School***.

Write an **expository essay** explaining **how the robotics club changed Lincoln Middle School and its students**.

Use information from the passage to describe at least **three ways the club made a difference**. Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write
questions.student_answer:
Do you think one small club started in a storage room can become one of the biggest and most infuential clubs of a middle school. Well Lincoln Middle School's roboitcs club started one year in a small storage closet with 8 optimistic students. Most of the students had never worked with robots but were excited to learn, they had guests like a local retired engineer that helped them troubleshoot and learn to think like enginners. And when it came to studying in class the teachers noticed that these students were more pacient when solving probelms and asked more questions. This club kept growing and became very exciting with more students joining and even more prizes joining too.

When the club was first created there was a small amount of students and  an even smaller room but they did great work with what they had. At first they started building robots borrowed kits and little skills. There first challenge was picking up small obejects with the robot. In the second paragraph of the passage they say "Students worked in pairs, testing motors and sensors". By Spring the were at there first competion allthough they did not win the brought home a teamwork award. But good word had gotten out about this new robotics club.

The robotics club had a local retired engennier come and volunteer to help the students think like inventors and learn to troubleshoot their robot. This helped the kids undersand problems and how to solve them in efficent and new ways that could improve the robot. In the 3rd paragraph of the passage they quote "More importantly they returned with new ideas and confidence". This was said after they did not win the regional championship but it shows how there new mindset lets them grow and accept failure. After they returned from the competition many new students were interested in the robotics club which brought new kids, space and materials.

Teachers also noticed a change in the robotics students. These students were more persitent and pacient when it came to solving problems in class. The robotics students asked more questions when it came to new assignments and were more eager to help other students. As stated in the last paragraph of the passage they say "Former students have gone on to study engineering and computer science". This shows how these students that started in the robotics club developed critical skills that helped them study Eninnering .

The Lincoln Middle School robotics club still runs to this day and is one of the most popular clubs at the school. Many students have joined and helped the team grow from no wins to almost a dozen. All of this was built off those first 8 students had a great vision. In the end the Lincoln roboics club is very sucessful and will go on to keep wining for many more years.
questions.feedback: Your essay has the shape the prompt asked for: a hook, three body paragraphs, and a conclusion, and your best moments are where you explain a quotation instead of repeating it, such as "it shows how their new mindset lets them grow and accept failure" and "developed critical skills that helped them study engineering." Three changes would raise the score. First, proofread for spelling: influential, robotics, engineers, patient, problems, objects, competition, although, engineer, understand, efficient, persistent, engineering, successful, winning, and "their" (not "there") first competition. Second, your first body paragraph tells how the club started rather than how it changed the school; turn it into a change, for example, how building and failing together taught teamwork, which the teamwork award proves. Third, use only what the passage says: it does not mention "almost a dozen" wins or students being "more eager to help other students," and claims like these cost you credibility with a reader who has the text. Finally, reread two sentences aloud and fix them: "At first they started building robots borrowed kits and little skills" and "All of this was built off those first 8 students had a great vision," and add the question mark to your opening question.

For a long period of time, many people have played a game so called Pokémon.

The game originated from Satoshi Tajiri. he yearned of creating a game that was interesting and exciting.

As a child, Tajiri enjoyed insects. He would spend hours trying to catch one. He loved them so much his friends called him "Dr. bug."

He would always say, "Every new bug was a mystery." Collecting bug made him feel rewarded.

When he grew older, he enjoyed playing video games. He learned coding to make his own games. He thought most games were boring and not exciting enough.

He wanted to make something everybody could enjoy. He remembered about his old insect collection and decided to use that as insperation.

He then created a game. In the game, players look for characters called Pokémon. There were over 150 Pokémon to collect.

Players threw Pokéballs at the little creatures and would catch them. Players could also trade with eachother.

The game had a slogan, and that was "Gotta catch 'em all!" For Tajiri, Pokémon were just like collecting bugs. He wished that players would feel the same happiness he felt as a kid.

The game became a very big thing, selling millions of copies. It then turned into a card game, an and app, and then a TV show. It even became a movie!

Tajiri turned a love for bugs, into an amazing game that to this day, is still popular.

**Prompt**

In the passage "Dive into a Sunken Museum" by Gail Skroback Hennessey, readers learn about artist Jason deCaires Taylor's unusual underwater sculptures.

Write **a well-organized paragraph** explaining why Jason chose to place his sculptures under the sea.

Your paragraph should:

- clearly state your central idea
- organize your writing
- develop your ideas in detail
- use evidence from the selection in your response
- use correct spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and grammar
questions.student_answer:
An artist named Jason deCaires Taylor has created over 500 life-size statues. But these are not normal statues, they are under the sea!

Jason has created two statue parks under the Caribbean Sea. The first one has 65 statues, it's nearby Grenada. The other one, in Cancun, Mexico, has almost 500 statues. It holds the record for the largest underwater statue park ever.

If you want to see these amazing statues up close, you must bring scuba or snorkel gear. Or if you don't want to get wet, You can also take a glass-bottom boat.

Why make statues under the sea you ask? Jason wants to protect coral reefs. Every single year, many swimmers go under and visit the reefs. But when admiring them, they accidently hurt them without knowing it. So if people swin to the statues instead, the reefs will be safe.

A seven-year-old kid named Sam Clarke decided to visit the park in Grenada. 'I wore a mask and snorkel,' Sam said. 'On my feet I wore fins that helped me swim.'

Sam saw a lot of statues. His favorite was the Circle Of Children. It is twenty-six children including both boys and girls stand in a circle, Holding hands under the ocean.

If you take a look at the statues faces, you can spot that have their eyes closed. That is because the children who posed for the statues had to keep their eyes closed while Jason made the mold. It took two hours.

Not long after, they were put into the ocean. Soon after, ocean life began to take them over and climb onto the statues and cover them. Sponges and seaweed grew on them, and many fish started to visit. After a while, life took over the statues.

And was Jason bothered by the sea life covering his art? 'No,' Jason says. 'I like it most of all. Each visit is new, because the sea changes the art.'

Sam loved the trip so much! 'Snorkeling in the statue park was great,' Sam said. 'I saw fish, cool statues, and even a man on a bike!'
questions.feedback: “Jason wants to protect coral reefs” clearly answers the question, and you explain that swimmers can hurt the reefs without meaning to. To make your paragraph stronger, put that important reason first and leave out extra details about Sam and the statues, since they do not explain why Jason put them underwater. For example, you could write, “Jason placed his sculptures under the sea so swimmers would visit the statues instead of accidentally hurting the coral reefs.”

analysis.pattern_summary: Jaxon's constructed responses keep losing points on sentence-level control rather than ideas. He joins independent clauses with commas (comma splices in G3.1 Q1 and Q4 and G3.5 Q4, Q8 and Q10). He writes fragments when asked for complete sentences (G3.2 Q6 and G3.5 Q9). He often ignores the required structure (an appositive, *since*, or *because/but/so*) and uses a different construction instead. He also loses points on proofreading (capitalization, possessives, "fund" for "found", "wa", "plaed") and on one-sentence explanations that lack a clear "because" reason or are wordy and unclear. His paragraphs are his strongest area (85–90%) but dropped to 65% in G3.5 for weak focus and extra details. Scores slid from 82–84% to 76% across five attempts, which suggests the same errors are repeating.
analysis.skill_gaps: comma splices/run-on correction, sentence fragments in short responses, appositive construction, following the specified conjunction (since/because/but/so), concise and non-redundant phrasing, "because" reasoning in one-sentence explanations, proofreading mechanics (capitalization, possessives, spelling, all-caps), paragraph focus and topic-sentence-first organization
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Jaxon is marked MASTERED in appositives, combining sentences, fragment vs. sentence, and paragraph writing, yet he still fails these same skills on tests (comma-spliced appositive attempts, fragments, ignored conjunctions). This suggests mastery came after only 1–2 attempts, mostly on recognition tasks, and does not transfer to independent written production or self-editing. The missing scores (best/latest = None) also mean we cannot confirm the mastery was strong.
analysis.rushing_impact: The one rushed test (G3.4, 80%) scored in line with his other attempts, so rushing probably had a minor effect, though the lowercase "layla", "fund" and other careless slips there may be partly speed-related.

analysis.pattern_summary: Josiah repeatedly loses points on one-sentence written responses because he gives a bare answer without a reason or explanation. This happens in G3.2 Q7 and Q9, G3.3 Q7, G3.4 Q6 and Q8, and G3.5 Q7, where feedback each time says to add a "because" reason. He also does not follow the specific skill the prompt names: he used "and" instead of "since" (G3.4 Q2), added a verb phrase instead of an appositive (G3.3 Q3), and used a participial phrase instead of a noun-phrase appositive (G3.5 Q4). Fragments that begin with "When…" (G3.3 Q7, G3.4 Q8, G3.4 Q9) and recurring spelling errors in paragraphs (impossable, storys, exiteing, fist, nomal) also hold back his scores. His paragraph responses score 60-95%, but the one-sentence items sit at 33-67%.
analysis.skill_gaps: Supporting an opinion with a reason (because-clauses), answering with a complete sentence rather than a "When…" fragment, writing true appositives (noun renaming), using subordinating conjunctions (since), following the exact skill named in the prompt, explaining the "why" in inference and character-trait questions, spelling and proofreading, subject-verb and grammar accuracy ("how take care"), and tying evidence to the question
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Josiah has MASTERED Basic Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Write Appositives, Combine Sentences With Appositives, and Fragment or Sentence in AlphaWrite, yet he still misses appositive and subordinating conjunction items and writes fragments on tests. This suggests the mastery does not transfer to open-ended written responses, probably because the quizzes are scaffolded or have few attempts (1 each), so he can pass them without being able to produce the skill independently.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data is given, but the incomplete reasoning, unfixed spelling, and fragments on short one-sentence items suggest that rushing or not proofreading may have contributed moderately, though the consistent skill-specific misses point to genuine gaps as well.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives Quiz, retake with open-response production (Production G3): he mastered it after one attempt, but he still writes verb phrases or participial phrases instead of noun-phrase appositives on tests, so he needs more independent practice.
- Combine Sentences Using Subordinating Conjunctions: since, because, when, after (Combining G3): he swapped "and" for "since" in G3.4 Q2 and needs practice using the specified conjunction.
- Elaborate Sentences With Reasons Using "Because" (Sentences G3): six of his one-sentence answers lacked a reason, so he should practice turning a claim into claim + because + evidence.
- Fragment or Sentence: Turn Fragments Into Complete Sentences (Sentences G3): he starts answers with "When…" and writes incomplete sentences, so he needs to rewrite fragments rather than only identify them.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer the Question Stem and Proofread Checklist: this would teach him to restate the prompt, confirm the required skill, and check spelling (impossible, stories, exciting, first, normal) before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across all three G3 tests, the student's ideas are generally on-topic, but short constructed responses (the 33-50% items) lose credit because they aren't written as complete, standalone sentences. Typical errors are fragments ("Because, it makes children happy."; "Listening to what guides tell you because..."), vague or unelaborated reasons ("it was nice," "The same idea but not with teddy bears"), and not following the directive (keeping "looked" when asked to change the verb). Capitalization and end punctuation errors recur in every test, including proper nouns, "I," and sentence starts ("hershey bears," "no," "yes," "i," "africa"). Missing spaces after periods and spelling slips also cost points even in the paragraph responses, which are otherwise strong (70-85%).
analysis.skill_gaps: complete sentence construction (fragments vs. full sentences), restating the question in the answer, elaborating reasons with specific evidence, following precise revision directions (verb replacement, conjunction combining), capitalization of proper nouns and sentence starts, end punctuation and spacing after periods, spelling and basic usage (its/it's, trevel, Garissa), pronoun and reference clarity, avoiding formulaic "One reason is… also" phrasing, concise sentence revision
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: No AlphaWrite data was included, so I can't identify which skills the student has mastered there. The test data does show a likely disconnect: the student can organize a multi-sentence paragraph (70-85% on the paragraph prompts) but doesn't reliably apply sentence-level mechanics and completeness on one-sentence responses. Check AlphaWrite completion and accuracy to confirm this.
analysis.rushing_impact: Only G3.3 was rushed, and it had the highest score (84%), so rushing likely had a modest effect. It may have contributed to the sloppy mechanics and the thin, formulaic answers on Q6-Q7, but the same errors appear in the non-rushed tests.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fragments vs. Complete Sentences (Sentences G2/G3): fixes the "Because, …" and "Listening to what guides tell you…" fragments by practicing subject plus predicate and turning fragments into full sentences.
- Answer the Question in a Complete Sentence (Writing Brainlift/Short Response): teaches restating the prompt stem so one-sentence answers stand alone (e.g., "The Teddy Bear Toss is popular because…").
- Capitalization and End Punctuation Editing (Grammar/Conventions G2-G3): targets repeated errors with proper nouns, "I," sentence starts, and missing periods or spaces after periods.
- Combine Sentences with Conjunctions (Sentences G3): builds on the Q2 "because" combining error and on punctuation within compound and complex sentences.
- Strengthen Verbs and Ela

analysis.pattern_summary: Julian's scores (78–84%) show a consistent plateau, not a collapse. The extended-response items drag him down through three recurring problems. (1) He does not execute the targeted sentence structure precisely. His "appositives" are actually a relative clause ("who made dinner") and a "where" clause, a vague appositive ("a way to study"), and a fragment with no verb ("Nearby, a caterpiller on a leaf"). His sentence combining also leaves gaps ("received the award the prestigious…") and creates comma splices. (2) He makes uncaught editing errors: missing or doubled words ("a place a place," "my mom shocked I," "it could the type"), tense and agreement slips ("ask," "by play," "task"), and spelling ("wated," "acheived," "nurteints," "storys"). (3) His Q11 paragraphs are generically organized but thin on specific text evidence, and he sometimes answers the wrong question (explaining "how" instead of "why" in G4.5 Q9). The G4.4 paragraph drew almost nothing from the article.

questions.prompt:
Passage referenced: "The Library on the Lake" (Stimulus S1).

Write an **expository essay** explaining how the new lakeside library changed life in the city.

Use information from the passage to describe at least three impacts (e.g., learning opportunities, cultural activities, local economy). Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragr
questions.student_answer:
In the article The Library on the Lake the new lakeside library integrates books, arts, and learning opportunities into a city that would not have had it otherwise. The library, a once forgotten warehouse, became a busy place for community life. The new library changes daily life in the city and proves that a good idea with careful planning can change the story of a place.

Firstly, this library, one that holds many books, serves as a place for citizens to read in silence. Consequently, it helps to educate the city and also provide stories of foriegn culture. According to the text, "Now, they surrounded shelves of books, small reading corners, and wide tables for study."

Furthermore, the library is a place that nurtures art and creative expression. For example, artists often paint along the walls, while musicians would play music in the open atrium. According to the text,"Local artists hung colorful paintings along the walls" and,"Musicians sometimes played in the open atrium."

Above all, the library provides learning opportunities and fun, educational activities or workshops. These workshops were made to nurture creativity for all ages. According to the text," Workshops... taught skills from boatbuilding to computer design.

In conclusion, the new library changes daily life in the city by providing books, arts, and learning opportunities. It changes a small, unnoticed city into a busy and lively travel destination. Citizens will likely continue to support and learn from their new library, because of the major impact that it has made on their daily life.
questions.feedback: Your essay clearly explains that the library improved city life through books, art, and workshops. The introduction gives a focused main idea, and each body paragraph stays centered on one impact. To make your explanation stronger, add a sentence after each piece of evidence that explains exactly how it changes life for residents. For example: “Because people can learn skills such as boatbuilding and computer design, the library helps residents gain useful knowledge and explore new interests.” Your conclusion effectively returns to the idea that the library made the city more active and lively.

questions.student_answer:
In the article Don't Give Up on Broccoli, the author explains how people's food preferences change over time. They explain that with three main reasons: the flavor window, taste-flavor learning, and social learning, which all have their different effects on us. All three contribute to our developing food preferences and are the primary reasons for our changing taste buds.

Firstly, the flavor window, a period from four to six months of age when babies are most open to trying new foods, is when we begin to shape our likes and dislikes about different foods. Although the window gradually closes, it has been proven to reopen later in life, leading to changes in our preferences later on in life. According to the text,"Offering a variety of flavors during this stage helps infants accept unfamiliar tastes later in life."

Secondly, taste-flavor learning is a way of connecting foods we already like to new and unfamiliar ones. This allows for us to combine something we already like with something that we are unceartain about, which helps us learn to like new flavors. According to the text,"Scientists have identified three ways people learn to like flavors... The second is taste-flavor learning,"

Finally, social learning is based on the idea that people tend to enjoy what friends and family enjoy. For example, babies whose mothers drank carrot juice are more likely to enjoy carrot flavored foods, which proves that social learning can teach us to like or dislike new flavors. According to the text,"People tend to enjoy what friends and family enjoy even beginning before birth."

In conclusion, our food preferences are mainly shaped by three parts that each contribute to our ever-growing taste buds. Through the flavor window, taste-flavor learning, and social learning, our food-related likes and dislikes continue to develop from ages one to 100. People all around the world continue to eat and discover new foods because our taste buds never stop growing!
questions.feedback: You clearly explain how the flavor window, taste-flavor learning, and social learning shape food preferences, and your carrot-juice example is especially strong. Your introduction gives a focused main idea, and each body paragraph stays centered on one way tastes develop. To make the essay flow more smoothly, use transitions that show how the ideas connect instead of only “Firstly,” “Secondly,” and “Finally”; for example, write, “As people grow older, taste-flavor learning can continue changing preferences after the flavor window closes.” Your conclusion effectively brings the three ideas together and reinforces that food preferences can keep changing throughout life.

questions.student_answer:
In the article A Day in the Life Aboard the International Space Station, the author explains how astronauts adapt their daily routines to life aboard the ISS. By adapting their basic hygiene, scientific research, and excercise practices, these astronauts work through the challenges of daily life in space. Although life on the ISS is very different from life on Earth, astronauts rely on their adapted routines to stay focused and safe.

To remain clean, astronauts adapt their basic hygiene despite the difficulties of microgravity. They do this by using items like pouches for water to wash their hands or no-rinse soap to clean themselves. According to the text," Water floats in small drops, so astronauts squeeze it into pouches and wipe themselves with no-rinse soap."

Due to the special experiments that microgravity offers, astronauts spend a large part of each day on scientific research. They adapt their research to microgravity by using special wires, tubes, and instruments that are secured to the cabin so that they don't float away. According to the passage," Wires... are secured so they do not drift around the cabin."

Finally, to remain strong and active throughout the day, excercise is essential for astronauts when in space. Engineers adapt excercising equipment by securing them to the floor and walls, allowing astronauts to excercise frequently. According to the article," Astronauts work out... using a treadmill with a harness, a stationary bicycle, and a resistance device."

In conclusion, astronauts use their adapted routines to manage their daily life outside of Earth. By changing the way they clean themselves, study and perform research, and excersise, astronauts stay focused and safe despite their adapted lives. Astronauts prove that adaptability and hard work make it possible to live and work while orbiting far above the planet.

Use information from the passage to describe at least **three ways the club made a difference**. Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic s
questions.student_answer:
There have been schools that have introduced a robotics club to their extracarricular activities. The robotics club changed Lincoln middle school in three major ways.

The First way the robotics club changed Lincoln Middle School and its students is by teaching students in the robotics club how to problem solve better. I know this because the author stated in the text "A retired engineer from the neighborhood volunteered to help, teaching them how to troubleshoot problems and think like inventors." This shows how impactful the robotics club was on students ability to problem solve, which may lead to better designs and ability to fix different problems.

The second major way the robotics club changed Lincoln Middle School and its students is by improving the way students are learning. The text stated "Teachers reported that club members asked more questions in science class and showed greater patience when solving problems." This shows that the robotics club impacts other aspects of school, not just robotics and inventing.

The third and final way the robotics club improved Lincoln Middle School and its students is by opening new doors for students and their career paths. The  text showed that "Former members have gone on to study engineering and computer science." This shows that because of the robotics club, members found successful career paths that they may otherwise have not found.

Lincoln Middle School, along with its students, was improved by the robotics club due to the robotics club helping students understand problem solving and inventing, helping them learn more effectively as they were prompted to ask more questions about problem solving, and it opened up new career paths for members of the club. Based on this, more schools should be making the addition of a robotics club to their school.
questions.feedback: You clearly explain three important changes caused by the robotics club: stronger problem-solving, better learning habits, and new career paths. Your quotations from the passage are well chosen, and you explain how each one supports your point. To make the essay flow more smoothly, use more varied transitions instead of relying mostly on “The First,” “The second,” and “The third.” For example, you could begin a paragraph with “Beyond improving problem-solving skills, the club also helped students become more engaged in science class.” Your conclusion effectively brings your three main ideas together and leaves the reader with a final thought about other schools starting robotics clubs.

**Write 5 clear para
questions.student_answer:
Going to space is a dream of many people's. Some people have disablities that would prevent them from doing so, but that didn't stop Michaela Benthaus. Michaela Benthaus's journey to space shows that determination and technology can break barriers.

The first way this is shown is by making changes to equipment to allow someone like Benthaus, who is in a wheelchair, to be able to ride in a rocket and make it to space. The text shows that with the help of Blue Origin, a slide for moving between a wheelchair and a seat, a strap to hold her legs in place, and a strong seat to support her would allow her to fly in a rocket ship and actually go into space. Without this change, Benthaus would not be able to do this.

The next way this is done is by programs that allow individuals to learn on the topic of space engineering, despite any disabilities they may have. The text shows that "She kept studying engineering and joined a training program with the European Space Agnecy in 2024." Because of this program, Benthaus was able to defy the setbacks of her disability and become an astronaut.

The third and final way this is done is by the use of an advanced piece of technology, the New Shepard. The text stated "Michaela Benthaus became the first person in a wheelchair to travel to space. The 33-year old German engineer launched from West Texas on Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket." Without this rocket, it is likely that Benthaus would have never been to space, meaning that not only would she not have a record, but she also wouldn't have been able to fulfill her dreams.

Michaela Benthaus's journey to space truly showed how determination and technology can take people to great measures. She made it to space as the first person in a wheelchair to do so with the power of advanced technology, engineering, and time learning and working hard. Benthaus's trip to space might not be the last as her hard work and dedication may have opened up doors for others.

skills.skill: Production G3 Combine Sentences With Appositives Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: Knox stays in the loop mainly because of sentence-combining tasks. He cannot construct appositives (G3.1, G3.5, G3.6, where he adds "just like Harry Potter/skunks" as a comma splice instead of a naming phrase). He also misuses subordinating conjunctions (*since*, *because*), reversing cause and effect or substituting "and" or "but" for the one requested. On short and extended responses he repeatedly makes verb tense and subject-verb agreement errors ("she remember," "porcupine lift," "help it stand out") and many spelling and capitalization errors. He rarely adds reasons or examples unless the prompt requires them, and he drifts off topic with unrelated comparisons ("just like birds," "just like skunks"). In G3.5 and G3.6 he also fails basic transformations such as turning a statement into a question, where he wrote "Where the books sold…" with no verb inversion and no question mark.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, comma splices/run-ons, subordinating conjunction logic (because/since cause-effect direction), sentence combining with a specified conjunction, statement-to-question transformation, verb tense consistency, subject-verb agreement, spelling and proofreading, capitalization and end punctuation, staying on topic and avoiding off-topic analogies, adding reasons/examples to explanations, concise sentence revision (removing redundancy), paragraph elaboration with text evidence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows Knox as MASTERED in Combine Sentences, Combine Sentences With Appositives, Kernel Expansion, and Fragment or Sentence, yet he still fails appositive and conjunction combining on every test (G3.1, G3.5, G3.6). Mastery on the quiz does not carry over to written production, and with no recorded best or latest scores and only 1 attempt per skill, the mastery flags may reflect shallow or lenient completion.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of the five tests (G3.1, G3.2, G3.5) were flagged as rushed, and his many careless errors (missing verbs, "teh," unproofread tense) suggest rushing contributed meaningfully, but the same appositive and conjunction errors recur on the non-rushed tests (G3.4, G3.6), so rushing is a significant but not sole cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): re-do with a higher mastery threshold and multiple attempts, since he keeps writing comma-spliced "just like…" additions instead of a naming phrase beside the noun.
- Combine Sentences Using Because, But, So (Sentences G3): targeted practice on cause-and-effect direction and on using the exact conjunction requested (*because*, *since*).
- Question Transformation / Sentence Types (Sentences G3): practice turning statements into questions with correct verb inversion and punctuation.
- Verb Tense and Subject-Verb Agreement Editing (Conventions G3): fix recurring errors like "she remember," "porcupine lift," and "help it stand out."
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): redo with a proofreading checklist (spelling, capitals, tense) and a requirement to add a reason or example with text evidence.

analysis.pattern_summary: Kolton's scores rose from 68% to 71% to 87%, but he keeps missing the top score band on extended-response items. His main problems are elaboration (the "why" or "how" behind an idea), staying on the prompt, and editing conventions. Across G5.1 and G5.2, one-sentence responses were often vague, off-task, or did not answer the question asked (e.g., "I would move to Africa," or a story about a friend's worm drawings that never says how someone feels). Meanwhile, he makes small repeated errors in spelling, contractions ("we we're," "firt," "nemisis," "identicall"), and punctuation. His paragraphs (Q11 across all three tests) have a clear main idea but lack specific text evidence, and their transitions and mechanics are inconsistent.
analysis.skill_gaps: elaboration and reasoning ("because" explanations), staying on prompt and answering the exact question, text evidence integration in paragraphs, descriptive appositive phrases, sentence revision for clarity and flow (transitions), proofreading for spelling and contractions, punctuation and run-on control in long single sentences, tone and seriousness in responses, reading-based inference responses (theme and cause/effect)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Kolton has mastered AlphaWrite skills such as Kernel Expansion, Subordinating Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, and Write Paragraph From Prompt, yet he still loses points on tests for elaboration, text evidence, and proofreading. The disconnect is that AlphaWrite checks skills in isolation with scaffolding. The tests require him to apply them independently, to a reading passage, and with self-editing. The AlphaWrite scores also show as None%, so mastery may reflect completion rather than depth.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing is not indicated in the data, but the many small, careless errors (e.g., "we we're," a missing period, an unclosed parenthesis) and off-topic or joking answers suggest limited proofreading and engagement, which likely cost a moderate number of points rather than being the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G5): his G5.1 appositive was basic ("the teacher") and lacked descriptive detail, so he needs practice writing appositives that add vivid details.
- Kernel Expansion with "Because/Why" Elaboration (Sentences G5): his short answers on inference and theme items lack reasons, so this would train him to expand a claim with an explanation.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with Text Evidence (AlphaWrite Paragraphs G5): his Q11 paragraphs name a main idea but skip specific article details, so he should practice citing and explaining evidence.
- Revise and Edit Your Own Writing / Proofreading Checklist (Writing Brainlift): recurring spelling, contraction, and punctuation errors need a routine for self-checking before submitting.
- Write Sentence From Prompt: Stay on Task Responses (Sentences G5): his off-topic answers (moving to Africa, the worm-drawing story) show he needs practice answering the exact question asked, in a sincere and focused way.

analysis.pattern_summary: Kylen's paragraph writing is often solid (Q11 scores of 60-90% on most tests), but short-response and sentence-level items keep dropping to 33-67% because of recurring errors. The main errors are starting answers with "Because" so they become fragments (G3.2, G3.6, G3.9, G3.14), not following the exact task instruction (using "so" when asked for "because," or a run-on or "because" sentence when asked for an appositive), and missing basic mechanics (capitalization, end punctuation, commas, spelling). In the latest tests (G3.13, G3.14, G3.1), blank or near-blank responses on the Q11 paragraph and other items pulled scores to 36-49%, which suggests disengagement or low persistence, not just skill gaps.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (still joining with "because" or a comma splice), answering in complete sentences instead of "Because..." fragments, restating the question stem in the answer, following the specific conjunction or task directive, run-ons and comma splices (missing commas before "so" or "then"), proofreading for capitalization, end punctuation, and spelling, text-evidence explanation (quoting the text instead of explaining why), staying on the question's subject (fans vs. team, or the character's motive), and writing stamina and completion on paragraph responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Kylen has mastered every AlphaWrite skill-plan item, including appositive production, basic conjunctions, combining sentences, and paragraph writing, yet keeps missing the same skills on tests (appositives scored 0-50% on G3.4, G3.5, G3.7, G3.8, G3.9, G3.10, G3.11, G3.12, G3.14, G3.1). The quizzes may be passed through recognition or scaffolding and not transfer to independent, unprompted writing, and mastery does not carry over to proofreading or to complete-sentence habits on open-ended items.
analysis.rushing_impact: The rushed tests (G3.6 at 71%, G3.9 at 72%, G3.13 at 36%) likely hurt moderately to heavily, because the "Because..." fragments and the blank or truncated answers (e.g., "Som" and empty Q11 responses) are the kinds of errors that carelessness and low effort produce, so G3.13 is probably mostly a rushing and effort effect.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives, retake with independent production (Production G3): appositives are still missed on nearly every test despite "mastery," so re-verify with unscaffolded items, including commas around the appositive.
- Write Appositives (Production G3): practice distinguishing an appositive from a "because" clause or a comma splice, since Kylen defaults to those.
- Complete Sentence Answers / Restate the Question (Writing Brainlift): drill turning "Because..." fragments into full sentences by reusing the question stem, which would fix recurring fragments on short-response items.
- Basic Conjunctions Targeted Practice: because/but/so (Sentences G3): practice following the specified conjunction and adding the comma before "so" and "then" to stop the run-ons and wrong-connector errors.
- Proofread and Revise Checklist (Writing Brainlift): a short self-edit routine for capitalization, end punctuation, and spelling before submitting, plus a "never submit blank" completion expectation for paragraph items.

analysis.pattern_summary: Lathan keeps missing the same short-response items that require a specific sentence structure. Appositive items scored 50% or lower on G3.3, G3.5, G3.6 and G3.7, and he answered with adverbs, "because," "and," or commas instead, or misidentified the appositive entirely ("Became," 0%). He also misses the exact directive in a prompt (stronger verb, "because/but/so," explain why), and his one-sentence responses often leave out the "why" or are not complete sentences. His paragraph scores are stronger (65–85%), but they follow a formula and carry mechanical errors (its/it's, apostrophes, capitalization, "i", "Thats"). The loop is therefore driven by precision on sentence-level tasks, not by paragraph writing.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive recognition and construction, following the specific directive in a prompt, sentence combining with a required conjunction (because/but/so), strong verb substitution, explaining "why" in one-sentence responses, complete-sentence construction, possessive vs. contraction (its/it's), apostrophes and capitalization, comma placement, using the text to support a cause-and-effect explanation, paragraph conclusions that go beyond restating the topic sentence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Lathan has mastered the G3 appositive (Write Appositives, Combine Sentences With Appositives) and conjunction quizzes in AlphaWrite, yet he still scores 50% or lower on the same skills on tests, which suggests the skills do not transfer to unscaffolded, test-format prompts. AlphaWrite also shows no best or latest scores, so "mastered" may reflect completion or attempt counts instead of real fluency, and the mastery signal is unreliable.
analysis.rushing_impact: Four of the five tests were flagged as rushed, and the repeated careless errors (missed directives, punctuation slips, a one-word answer for the appositive question) suggest rushing contributed substantially, though the consistent appositive failures show a real skill gap beneath it.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives (Production G3): re-run it with a no-scaffold, timed format, because he mastered it but still writes adverbs or "because" clauses instead of renaming noun phrases.
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G3): practice on short passages in test-style wording ("Combine using an appositive"), since he substitutes "and" or "because" for the appositive.
- Basic Conjunctions (Sentences G3): drill because/but/so with prompts that require a specific conjunction, because he used "and" when told to use because/but/so.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): practice answering the prompt's exact "why" or "how" question with evidence and a real concluding sentence, to fix one-sentence responses that skip the reason.
- Writing Brainlift revision/editing activity on mechanics (its/it's, apostrophes, capitalizing "I," complete sentences): a slow, checklist-based proofread before submitting, to cut the recurring conventions errors and the rushing.

analysis.pattern_summary: On the G3.1 test, the student gave single-letter answers ("as," "z," "g," "h," "j") to Q1-Q6, which cover appositive combining, question conversion, sentence revision, conjunction combining, fragment repair, and opinion writing. That produced a 20% score, so the skills were mostly untested rather than proven weak. questions.student_answer:
People help monarch butterflies stay alive by building way stations, donating money, and taging butterflies.

The first way that people can help monarch butterflies stay alive are way stations.Way stations are a small garden where monarchs could rest and lay eggs. It's a perfect place for butterflies to rest for birth. It's very important to have way stations so that butterflies can birth healthy eggs.

The next way that people can support monarch butterflies is donating money to monarch butterfly stations. This donated money is used for building way stations, and places to help butterflies rest and stay healthy. These donations are super important so that the butterfly population doesn't get extinct.

The last way people can help monarchs stay alive is by tagging butterflies. People tag butterflies with small stickers, count caterpillars, and record monarch sighting. This can help people see how the monarch butterfly population is doing and how people can help support them more. In conclusion, building way stations, donating money, and tagging can really impact the monarch population in a great way.

analysis.pattern_summary: Nathaniel's extended-response essay (Q11) has improved from 50% to 75% to 80%, but it still falls short of passing because he does not explain his text evidence. He drops in quotes without saying *why* they prove his point, and his elaboration is vague. On G6.3 he picked "Citizen scientists help monarchs by doing things" as the best elaboration and put a comma before "because", so he misses what makes elaboration specific and how subordinating conjunctions are punctuated. Frequent spelling errors ("perventing," "habait," "trackeing," "animted," "wining") and an unparallel, run-on thesis list ("way station, perventing habait loss, and trackeing them, so you can…") also keep the essays from earning full marks.
analysis.skill_gaps: Analysis and explanation of text evidence (quote → "why it matters"), specific elaboration (replacing vague words like "things" with concrete details), punctuation with subordinating conjunctions (no comma before mid-sentence "because"), parallel structure in thesis and lists, essay organization (topic sentences, separate body paragraphs, conclusion), proofreading and spelling of high-frequency and content words, sentence boundaries and clarity in thesis statements
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Nathaniel is marked MASTERED in Basic and Subordinating Conjunctions, Elaborate Paragraphs, Kernel Expansion, and Turn Outline Into Draft, yet he still misses "because" punctuation and elaboration questions on the test and writes vague, unexplained evidence in his essays. This suggests he passes the isolated drills but does not transfer the skills to timed, independent writing. The AlphaWrite score fields are also blank (None%), so mastery may have come from very few attempts, with 1–2 attempts per skill.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a moderate effect: both MC misses on G6.3 (conjunction punctuation and elaboration) and the many careless spelling errors in the G6.1 and G6.3 essays look like the result of skipping proofreading, though the persistent evidence-explanation gap appears even in the non-rushed G6.2 test.
analysis.recommended_activities:
1. Elaborate Paragraphs, revisit with explain-the-evidence focus (AlphaWrite G6): he is marked mastered but still writes vague elaboration ("doing things"), so he needs practice turning general statements into specific, evidence-backed details.
2. Subordinating Conjunctions: Punctuation Review (AlphaWrite G6): he placed a comma before "because" in a mid-sentence clause, so he needs to practice when commas are and are not required.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across G3.2–G3.4 (scores 76%, 71%, 82%), Phoenix loses points on tasks that require following a specific sentence-level instruction. These include identifying sentence type (Q4 "Imperative" for a declarative sentence), adding an appositive (Q3), supplying a sentence-opening subordinating conjunction (Q5), and swapping in a stronger verb (Q1, where he added adjectives instead). Written responses also stay stuck at about 67%. He names a detail or opinion but does not explain the "why" or "how" (Q7 G3.3, Q6/Q9/Q10 G3.4), and he repeatedly leaves out capitalization, apostrophe use, and spelling ("familly," "fish boxs," "seal's," "visitng," "pokmon"). His paragraphs follow a formulaic "This shows how…" ending with thin elaboration, and his Q10 answer in G3.4 ("leaving cool souvenirs") was inaccurate and showed weak comprehension of the text.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, sentence type identification (declarative vs. imperative), subordinating conjunctions and sentence openers, strong or precise verb choice, explaining reasoning (the "because/why" step), elaborating text evidence beyond restating it, capitalization and proofreading, spelling, possessive vs. plural apostrophe use, subject-verb agreement and grammar in paragraphs, reading comprehension of the stimulus text
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Phoenix has mastered nearly every G3 AlphaWrite skill, including appositives, change sentence type, basic conjunctions, and elaborating paragraphs, yet he still misses these same skills on tests (appositive Q3, sentence type Q4, conjunction Q5, elaboration in Q6/Q7/Q9/Q10). The mastery is not transferring: he likely passes structured quiz formats but does not apply the skills independently, or does not proofread and reread the prompt on open-ended test items. The AlphaWrite data also shows best/latest scores as None, so the mastery evidence is weak.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided, but the careless errors (missing capitals, typos, answering a different task than asked, such as adding adjectives instead of changing the verb) suggest that rushing or lack of proofreading likely cost him several points, though it probably does not explain the repeated pattern of missing "why" elaboration.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives / Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G3 and Sentences G4): re-practice with fresh items and a stricter, transfer-style format, since he missed the test appositive despite "mastery."
- Change Sentence Type (Transformation G3, plus a sentence-type identification review): fix the declarative vs. imperative confusion and reinforce reading the sentence before classifying.
- Elaborate Paragraphs / Use Three Strategies (Paragraphs G3, then G4 equivalents): train him to add a "because" or "for example" explanation after each claim and to explain how evidence supports the point instead of restating it.
- Basic Conjunctions / Subordinating Conjunctions (Combining G3, G4): practice choosing the right opening word (because, although, since) for sentence-starter items like Q5.
- Writing Brainlift proofreading and revision routine (capitalization, spelling, apostrophes, subject-verb agreement): add a required self-check before submitting any written response.

Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Quentin's written responses give a correct main idea but leave out the "because" reasoning and text evidence. On Q6, Q9, and Q10 of G3.4, graders asked him to add a reason or detail from the passage, and each scored 67%. On the paragraph-level prompts (G3.4 Q11 at 50%, G3.5 Q11 at 20%), he wrote one or two thin sentences with no opening, supporting details, or conclusion. Recurring mechanical errors (missing capitals, apostrophes, spelling such as "listining" and "sculports", and run-together words such as "thenbook") also keep him from full credit. His score fell from 71% to 60%, and the 20% on the paragraph task shows that extended writing is the main barrier.
analysis.skill_gaps: elaboration with reasons ("because" explanations), text evidence integration, paragraph structure (topic sentence, supporting details, conclusion), extended paragraph stamina and development, answering the full prompt (both parts of a two-part question), capitalization and apostrophe use, spelling and proofreading, word spacing
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Quentin shows every G3 paragraph and sentence skill as MASTERED (topic sentences, transitions, writing paragraphs from a prompt, combining sentences), usually after only 1 attempt and with no best/latest scores recorded. Yet he still fails to write a full paragraph on tests, so the mastery is probably shallow and does not transfer to independent, text-based writing. He did correctly build the appositive on G3.5 Q4, but the 50% there suggests the mastery was not reliable.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.4 test was flagged as rushed, and the missing reasons, capitalization, and spelling errors are the kind rushing causes, but the G3.5 test was not rushed and he did worse (60%, with 20% on the paragraph), so rushing was a minor factor compared with the underlying skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): repeat it with a text-based prompt and a quality threshold, since his G3.5 Q11 paragraph (20%) lacked structure and detail.
- Write Cs From Details (Paragraphs G3): practice writing concluding sentences, because his paragraphs end abruptly with no closing idea.
- Write Ts From Details (Paragraphs G3): practice opening sentences that restate the prompt and set up a paragraph, a step he skips on the extended-response items.
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): redo it with a scored attempt to confirm the skill holds, since he only got 50% on the G3.5 appositive item.
- Writing Brainlift "Because" Elaboration and Text Evidence Practice (Writing Brainlift): use sentence frames ("___ because the text says ___") to add the reason and passage detail that graders requested on Q6, Q9, and Q10.
- Writing Brainlift Proofreading Checklist (Writing Brainlift): a short routine for capitals, apostrophes, spelling, and word spacing before submitting.

questions.prompt:
**Prompt**

Read the passage “The Life of a Porcupine”. Write **one well-organized paragraph** on the following:

**Explain how the porcupine’s body helps it stay safe in the wild.** Use facts from the passage in your answer.

Your paragraph should:

1. Clearly state your central idea

2. Organize your writing

3. Develop your ideas in detail

4. Use evidence from the selection in your response

5. Use correct spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and grammar

Make sure to:

1. Review the selec
questions.student_answer: Porcupines bodies help them stay safe in the wild in various ways. One way they stay safe are their quills. A porcupine has over 30,000 quills that are long stiff hairs that protect them from enemies. If a hungry predator comes too close, it will first give a warning, but if it doesn't follow it then the porcupine will whirl around and poke them with their tail. Another way their bodies help them stay safe is their grip. Their long claws and rough paws help them grip branches easier so they climb smoother. With this ability, they can eat buds, leaves, and bark from the trees. In the winter, when food is harder to find, they eat pine needles instead. Porcupines bodies look cool and protect them in various ways!
questions.feedback: “A porcupine has over 30,000 quills that are long stiff hairs that protect them from enemies” is a strong fact because you explain how the quills help keep the animal safe. You also organized your paragraph clearly by explaining its quills first and then its claws and paws. To make your writing even stronger, check grammar and possessive words: write “porcupines’ bodies,” not “porcupines bodies,” and make sure the subject and verb match. For example: “One way porcupines stay safe is by using their quills.”

skills.skill: Paragraph From Prompt G3 Write Paragraph From Prompt Quiz
Production G3 Combine Sentences With Appositives Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: Rafaela's scores are 80-89%, but she keeps missing the short-response items that test sentence-level mechanics. Her most frequent error is the comma splice or run-on, seen in G3.2 Q9, G3.5 Q4, G3.6 Q7, and G3.7 Q1, Q2, Q3, Q8 and Q9. Appositive items (G3.3 Q3, G3.5 Q4 and Q5, G3.6 Q3) are also persistently weak: she swaps in "but," names a verb as the appositive, and writes a fragment. Her paragraphs are organized (75-90%), but she often stops short of explaining reasons (G3.4 Q10, Q6), and she makes careless errors with capitalization, "i," spelling, and misplaced commas ("so," with a comma).
analysis.skill_gaps: comma splices/run-on sentences, appositive identification and construction, combining sentences with conjunctions (comma + FANBOYS), sentence completeness (fragments and missing verbs), one-sentence responses that stay within the "one sentence" constraint, explaining "why" in a response (reasoning elaboration), capitalization of "I" and proper nouns, proofreading and spelling, comma placement with conjunctions, using transition/sentence-starter words correctly (G3.3 Q5 "Later, there was...")
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Rafaela has mastered every AlphaWrite skill that matters here, including Basic Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Write Appositives, and Combine Sentences With Appositives, yet she still fails the same skills in test writing. The mastery does not transfer to open-ended, unprompted writing, where she does not self-edit and the quiz-format success is not carrying over. The AlphaWrite results also show no best/latest percentages, so mastery may reflect completion rather than depth.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing very likely contributed substantially, since four of the five rushed tests contain mostly careless errors (lowercase "i," misspellings like "pumpkings" and "knowm," comma splices) that she can already correct, and the one non-rushed test (G3.6) gave her highest score of 89%.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fix Run-Ons and Comma Splices (Sentences G3): she repeatedly joins two complete ideas with only a comma (G3.2 Q9, G3.6 Q7, G3.7 Q1, Q2, Q3, Q8, Q9).
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3): appositive combination and identification are repeatedly missed (G3.5 Q4, Q5; G3.6 Q3; G3.3 Q3) despite the AlphaWrite "mastery."
- Revise and Edit Your Own Writing / Proofreading Checklist (Writing Brainlift): she needs a routine to check capitalization, spelling, commas, and "one sentence" limits before submitting, which targets the rushed, careless errors.
- Fragments to Complete Sentences (Sentences G3): she needs practice making sure every sentence has a subject and a verb (G3.6 Q3, G3.7 Q1).
- Write Explanatory Sentences with Because/Why (Paragraphs G3): she tends to state an answer without explaining it (G3.4 Q6 and Q10), so she needs practice adding the reason or why.

analysis.pattern_summary: Robert's weakest area is the extended-response paragraph (Q11 on all three tests: 40%, 40%, 30%). He writes only a single topic or reason sentence, such as "Porcupines are interesting animals," and does not develop it with details or text evidence. His short responses also lack reasons and elaboration, and he misses specific sentence-level tasks: he used "and" instead of an appositive, wrote an ungrammatical question ("why we can't"), and made pronoun agreement errors ("it... their quills"). Scores of 64%, 69%, and 64% show he is stuck just below the passing threshold rather than getting worse.
analysis.skill_gaps: paragraph development and elaboration, integrating text evidence from passages, appositive phrases, question formation and word order, pronoun-antecedent agreement, adding reasons or "because" explanations, proofreading and spelling (e.g., "unde")
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Robert has mastered nearly every G3 AlphaWrite skill, including Elaborate Paragraphs, Write Paragraph From Prompt, Change Sentence Type, and Combine Sentences, yet he still writes one-sentence "paragraphs" and misses sentence-type and combining items on tests. This suggests he can pass the isolated, scaffolded activities but does not transfer the skills to independent, passage-based writing. The AlphaWrite scores are also all listed as None%, so mastery may reflect completion rather than real proficiency.
analysis.rushing_impact: Two of the three tests (G3.1 and G3.6) were rushed, which probably contributed to the short, unelaborated answers and grammar slips, but the same Q11 weakness appeared on the non-rushed G3.5 test, so rushing is only a partial cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): Robert wrote one-sentence responses to paragraph prompts on every test, so he needs to redo this activity with a requirement of at least 4-5 sentences and supporting details.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): have him do this with passage-based prompts that require text evidence, since he mastered it in isolation but not in the test format.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G4): he replaced the appositive with "and" on G3.5, so he needs direct instruction and practice with appositive construction.
- Change Sentence Type (Sentences G3): repeat with a focus on question word order (e.g., "Why can't we...?"), since mastery did not carry over to the G3.1 test.
- Writing Brainlift: Evidence-Based Paragraph Writing with a self-check (topic sentence, 2+ details, reason, proofread for agreement and spelling): this addresses transfer and rushing by building a revision habit before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Robert's scores on G4.1 and G4.2 were high (89% and 88%), yet he stayed in the loop. The short-response items (appositives, combining sentences, fragment repair) repeatedly earned only 33–75%, so the gap is in precise sentence-level construction. He writes the right ideas but makes errors in construction: he inserts a non-appositive phrase (a purpose phrase) in place of an appositive, misuses "but" where the ideas don't contrast, writes run-ons and comma splices ("my family they are pretty... and because"), and drops words ("going Chicago"). On G4.3 his paragraph was a single run-on with no organization (45%). His paragraph writing is strong when he's engaged (90–95% on G4.1 and G4.2), but it drops when he's under pressure or less engaged.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (distinguishing appositives from purpose phrases), choosing logical conjunctions (because/but/so) to show cause vs. contrast, run-on and comma-splice correction, sentence completeness and subject-verb structure when revising fragments, proofreading for dropped words and spelling/homophones (complement/compliment, someones), paragraph organization (topic sentence, evidence, closing) under independent timed conditions, sustained effort and completion on open-response items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Robert has mastered every listed AlphaWrite skill, including appositives, combining sentences, fragments, and paragraph writing, but he still misses the same skills on tests (appositives on G4.2 Q4 and G4.4 Q3, combining sentences on G4.1 Q5 and G4.4 Q4, fragment repair on G4.4 Q2). The disconnect is that the quizzes show only mastery status (no scores) and likely check recognition or guided practice, while tests require independent production, accuracy, and self-editing in context.
analysis.rushing_impact: G4.4 (33%) was rushed and 3 of 7 responses were blank, so rushing and disengagement probably account for most of the drop, though the non-blank answers still showed the same appositive and conjunction errors, which would have capped the score at about 50% per item.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives (Production G4): he confuses appositives with purpose or descriptive phrases, so he needs production practice with noun-renaming appositives placed right after the noun.
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G4): he needs to build appositives into combined sentences, since this is where tests keep catching him (G4.2 Q4, G4.4 Q3).
- Basic Conjunctions (Sentences G4): to practice choosing "because/but/so" by relationship (cause vs. contrast), which fixes the "but" error on G4.1 Q5 and the missing conjunction on G4.4 Q4.
- Fragment Or Sentence (Sentences G4): to practice repairing fragments while preserving the original meaning (G4.4 Q2 "student" for "study") and fixing run-ons.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraph G4): to rebuild topic sentence, evidence, and closing structure, since the G4.3 paragraph was one unorganized run-on. Add a timed proofreading checklist (dropped words, homophones, apostrophes) and a requirement to submit a response for every item.

questions.student_answer: Logos can be popular and common in everyday use. But if we see logos everyday, then why can we not remember them? About 10 years ago, in 2015, 85 students were asked to draw the famous apple logo. Though many of them thought they where right, only 1 of 85 of them could draw it correctly. Lots of the students missed miniscule details, like how many leaves are there and if it has a bite on the apple or not. This wasn't the onlytest that they did. In 1970, many people where requested to draw a perfect picture of the penny. Nearly all the people failed to excecute the perfect penny. Most forgot where the words where, how the face was drawn, and how to draw the little details. Logos are supposed to be easy to remember, with just a quick glance at it. But when we see them very often, our brains ignore the small details. This called "attentional saturation". Small details usaually get left out. This is also called gist memory. The gist is the big picture of the logo, not the little details. Overall, logos can be hard to remember, but you can still remember the big picture.
questions.feedback: “Our brains ignore the small details” is a strong passage-based idea because it clearly explains why people may not remember every part of a logo. analysis.pattern_summary: Ronan's content and ideas are mostly sound. He follows the task and includes relevant details, but he keeps losing points on mechanics and sentence-level control. These errors include missing helping verbs ("I always been"), homophone and spelling slips ("to nervous," "where/were," "togheter," "becuase"), run-together or garbled words ("stood of straightbut"), and missing end punctuation. On single-sentence tasks he also struggles to follow the exact syntactic directive (using "because" in G5.3 Q4, forming an interrogative in G5.3 Q5, which came out as an awkward tense-mismatched question). His explanatory responses (G5.1 Q8, G5.2 Q8) restate the prompt or stay vague rather than explaining cause and effect. Across the three tests he does not proofread, so errors that the grader flags as small repeat every time, and the scores (72%, 78%, 51%) stay short of the threshold.
analysis.skill_gaps: proofreading and self-editing, spelling and homophones (too/to, were/where, because), verb tense and helping verbs (past perfect "had"), end punctuation and spacing between words, following sentence-transformation directions (adding "because," interrogative conversion), cause-and-effect elaboration in single-sentence responses, combining sentences cleanly without garbling wording, avoiding circular or repetitive reasoning, paragraph polish and sustained effort on long responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Ronan has mastered every AlphaWrite skill listed, including Combining Basic Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Elaborate Paragraphs, and Paragraph From Prompt G5. Yet he still misses conjunction use ("because"), sentence combining, and polished paragraphs on tests, so the mastery is not transferring. The AlphaWrite quizzes show no scores (best/latest=None) with only 1-2 attempts each, which suggests mastery was reached with little practice, and none of the quizzes appear to test mechanics, proofreading, or following exact directions under test conditions.
analysis.rushing_impact: The rushed G5.3 test (51%) likely cost him a lot, since a blank Q11 (0%) and unfinished, directive-missing answers on Q4 and Q5 account for most of the drop from his 72-78% range on the earlier tests.

- Combine Sentences Using Because, But, So (Sentences G5): he missed the "because" directive in G5.3 Q4 and produced a garbled combined sentence in G5.1 Q3, so he needs more practice with conjunction-based combining.
- Verb Tense and Helping Verbs, Past Perfect (Grammar G5): "I always been" shows a gap in forming perfect tenses.
- Rewrite Sentence Types: Declarative to Interrogative (Sentences G5): he converted a statement to a question with the wrong tense and word order.
- Explain Cause and Effect in One Strong Sentence (Writing Brainlift): his single-sentence explanations (G5.1 Q8, G5.2 Q8) restate the prompt instead of explaining what happened or why. Pair this with a timed "Read, Plan, Write, Check" routine to prevent blank or rushed submissions.

analysis.pattern_summary: Sabrina keeps stalling on sentence-level transformation tasks (rewriting as a question or interrogative, combining sentences with a conjunction, and using an appositive). She often changes or drops words from the original, writes an exclamation instead of a question, or produces a general combined sentence rather than the required structure. Her paragraph responses (Q11) are also inconsistent: the 3.2 paragraph and the 3.6 porcupine paragraph score only 55% and 45%, because she writes everything in one run-on sentence or a short block without a topic sentence, a developed detail, or a closing sentence. Proofreading errors recur across tests: "buy" for "by," "charitys," "butterflys," "aniamls," "arguement," a missing space after a period, and "apartment" for "department." One blank response and the 33% on an inference question that needed a reason (Q6, G3.5) suggest she also struggles to explain reasoning and sustain effort on open-ended items.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, converting statements to questions/interrogatives while preserving the original wording, sentence combining with conjunctions and correct punctuation, following the exact task directive, paragraph structure (topic sentence, multiple supporting details, closing sentence), elaboration with reasons/text evidence, spelling and plural/word-form accuracy, proofreading, response stamina on open-ended items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Sabrina shows "MASTERED" in AlphaWrite for Change Sentence To Question, Write Appositives, Elaborate Paragraphs, and Using Transition Words, yet she still misses the same skills on tests (question conversion, appositives, paragraph development). Mastery was reached in a single attempt with no recorded scores, so it likely reflects shallow or guided practice that isn't transferring to independent, unscaffolded writing. The "mastered" flags may be unreliable.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably contributed moderately on G3.5 and G3.6, where careless errors (apartment/department, a stray comma, a single-sentence paragraph) and a lack of proofreading were evident, but the underlying structural gaps would likely keep her scores below mastery even without rushing.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3): re-do with a higher accuracy threshold and multiple attempts, since she turned the appositive item into a "because/as" clause rather than a renaming phrase set off by commas.
- Change Sentence To Question (Sentences G3): practice keeping the original wording and changing only the verb order, with an interrogative and exclamatory contrast, since she wrote an exclamation and changed "department" to "apartment."
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions (Sentences G3): focus on retaining all details ("golden spines") and punctuating correctly, since the G3.5 combination dropped a detail and misplaced a comma.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): redo with full-paragraph drafting that requires a topic sentence, 2-3 evidence-based details, and a closing sentence, since her porcupine and camel paragraphs were one or two run-on sentences.
- Proofreading and Editing Checklist (Writing Brainlift): a short routine (spelling, plurals, spacing after periods, rereading the prompt) before submitting, to reduce careless errors and rushed work.

skills.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Silver stays in the loop mainly because of thin, unsupported written responses. Across all three tests, graders repeatedly say "add a reason or example" for answers that are correct but bare (e.g., "The children are thankful for the books," "In the text Layla is kind," "The lesson is to be nice to others"). Text-evidence integration is the weakest area. Paragraph tasks (G3.2 Q11 at 30%, G3.4 Q11 at 60%) lack specific article details and are weakened by spelling and conventions errors ("Whiel we where," "feed," "betwen," "ploshon," "impotant," "grope," "there jobs"). Verb-choice precision was also weak (G3.4 Q1, "stomped at the flower" changed the meaning). Scores moved 62% → 82% → 69%, so the G3.3 pass was not sustained when the tasks demanded inference and explanation.
analysis.skill_gaps: Elaborating with a reason ("because") or example, text evidence integration, explaining character traits with support, paragraph development and organization (G3.4 Q11 lacks a clear topic sentence and relevant details), grade-level spelling and proofreading, homophone and word-form errors (where/were, there/their, feed/freed), precise verb choice and word meaning in context, expanding sentences with when/where/how details, sentence construction (missing "to" in "good idea name")
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Silver is marked MASTERED on "Identify Topic Sentence and Sequence Details" (Paragraphs G3), but only 1 attempt with no recorded score suggests thin evidence of mastery. Identifying a topic sentence is a recognition skill, so it doesn't transfer to producing a well-organized, evidence-based paragraph on tests (G3.4 Q11 scored 60%, G3.2 Q11 30%).
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data is provided, but the unedited spelling errors and consistently bare one-sentence answers suggest rushing or lack of revision may have contributed modestly; the main cause is a skill gap in elaboration and proofreading.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Add a Reason Using "Because" (Sentences G3): Silver's answers are clear but lack reasons, and graders flagged this on nearly every one-sentence response.
- Support an Answer with Text Evidence (Paragraphs G3): Silver gives generic claims ("Layla is kind," "children are thankful") without article details, which hurts the paragraph questions.
- Write a Paragraph with Topic Sentence, Details, and Concluding Sentence (Paragraphs G3): Silver needs practice producing, not just identifying, organized paragraphs with relevant details.
- Choose Stronger Verbs (Word Choice G3): Silver's "stomped at the flower" shows trouble matching verb meaning to context.
- Revise and Edit for Spelling and Conventions (Writing Brainlift): the repeated misspellings and homophone errors (where/were, there/their) need a proofreading routine before submitting.
